speechtext:
1.	How much has been realized from sale of surplus army stores since the Armistice?

2.	What was the initial cost of the property so sold?
3.	Were all sales made hy public auction dr public tender?

1.	$6,775,705.26; sold through the War Purchasing Commission.
2.	It is considered that it would be quite impossible to give even an approximately correct answer to question No. 2 as it now stands. The prices originally paid by the department for many of the surplus stores sold varied greatly from time to time. For instance, the prices paid by the department for army boots ranged from $4 to $6 during the term of the war, and the selling price bore no necessary relation to the cost price. This applies also to underwear, blankets, socks and many other items. It is possible to give the maximum and minimum prices originally paid for each article sold as surplus, but the record of the purchase of each article will have to be perused. It will take months to prepare such a statement.
3.	The War Purchasing Commission is responsible for the method of selling, and prices at which sales are made, and authorized the sales.
The answer in one word to the third question would be "no," but this would not give a fair impression as to the methods adopted for selling, and the following reply is therefore suggested:-
"Practically all goods have been offered for sale by tender. Advertisements were inserted in all daily and trade papers, and besides sending tender forms to those answering these advertisements, forms were also distributed over a wide mailing list covering all parts of Canada. The prices tendered, however, in some cases were so low that they had to be rejected and the goods offered for sale at a fixed price by circulars which were given a wide distribution.
"Since the end of January, sales have been largely conducted by price lists, as announced by advertisement.
"Sales at fixed prices have also been made to Dominion, Provincial and Municipal Government Departments, hospitals, charitable and philanthropic institutions, and to returned soldiers and sailors, widows and dependents of soldiers and sailors.
"Large advertisements informing the public as to the methods of sale were inserted in all daily and trade papers in the spring of 1919, early winter 1919, and February of this year."

Under the old classification, the maximum and minimum salaries of the letter carriers were $939 and $636 respectively. Under the new classification the maximum and minimum will be $1,260 and $780 respectively. Both these figures are apart from the bonus. In the application of the classification the letter carriers who were receiving the maximum of the old classification, namely, $939, receive under the new classification the' salary at the-scale next above that which they were receiving, namely, $1,020, so that all who were receiving $939, the maximum under the old classification, will start in at $1,020 under the new classification as of April 1, 1919. But where men had been in

Those who have not been in receipt of the maximum for five years will start in at $1,020. The delegation that waited on the Government represented men who had attained the maximum, but had not enjoyed it for a period of five years. They made two requests, first, that all who had attained the maximum under the old classification should immediately be given the maximum under the new. That is, they should be moved up from $939 to $1,260, as from April 1, 1919, which with the married man's bonus would make a total of $1,656 for last year, or in the alternative, if they did not get the maximum under the new classification as of 1st April, 1919, those who had attained the maximum under the old classification, whether they had served five years or notr should start in at $1,140 as from the 1st April, 1919, which would give them with the married man's bonus $1,656 for this year. The Government could not see its way clear to comply with either request, and so advised the letter carriers. As already intimated if they were married men or heads of households, they received in addition to salary, $420 as a bonus last year, if unmarried the single man's bonus, both of which will be continued during the current year. The men who waited on the Government will receive this year $1,140 in salary as they will move up one step in the classification owing to its being made retroactive to the 1st April, 1919, and, if they are married men or heads of households, they will be entitled to a bonus of $420, making their salary and bonus $1,560, and if unmarried, $1,332. I should like to inquire of the Government whether in view of the enormous increase in the cost of carrying on, it is intended to grant the rural mail carriers a bonus in addition to the price mentioned in the contracts which they' took a few years ago.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question
which my hon. friend has asked is one on which the Government has not been called upon to form an opinion this session, but I will explain the situation as I understand it. Where any contract was taken before the war or in the earlier years of the war, at a time when prices were substantially lower than they are to-day, the Post Office Department permits that contract to be re-advertised wherever the contractor desires that that should be done, and then a new contract is let, presumably at the current rates. I understand that in many cases the mail carriers have asked that their contracts should be terminated, and that advertisements should be issued and new tenders called for. In such cases new tenders have been called for, and when the new contract is made the old contract is terminated. So far as I am aware the Post Office Department has not up to this time seen its way clear to depart from that arrangement, which still prevails.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Ever since the war the department has been empowered by section 2 of the Dominion Lands Act to count the period of service of an enlisted man as residence on his homestead, and in the event of his coming back permanently disabled, so as not to be capable of working, to give him his patent; similarly, to give patent on behalf of the man who was killed or who died on active service. That privilege was extended statutorily to members of any of the allied forces, but, of course, the Department of Justice advised that members of the American army were not members of an allied force, and consequently they have had to be denied this special concession of section 2. The effect of this provision is simply to enable us to include them as well as members of any of the other allied forces, who are virtually in precisely the same position as the American army.

As a matter of curiosity rather than one of any importance, I may ask my hon. friend if there is any real line of distinction between the allied powers and the associated powers. All through fthe Peace Treaty they are spoken of as " The Allied and Associated Powers," and I do not know if we have had any precise definition as to the distinction, if there is a distinction.
It was the desire of the United States to be termed an associated power.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sure I do not know why they called themselves an "associated" rather than "allied" power, but inasmuch as they did, the provisions of the Act as it stood could not apply to members of the American army.
Do I understand that we are about to consolidate Bills 35 and 55 now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Not having at hand the Dominion Lands Act, may I ask the minister to be kind enough to explain the effect of the amendment made by section 2 of Bill 35?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Dominion Lands Act was amended a year ago so as to provide that an alien entrant, though he could not naturalize now under the Naturalization Act, could go before a judge and obtain a certificate to a certain effect set out in the Act, that he was entitled to naturalization but for the provisions of the new section of the Naturalization Act; and if he were not entitled to naturalization under the law apart from that provision, the judge would certify why he was not so entitled. That had to be done; otherwise a man who came . in here under a certain state of the Naturalization Act and took homestead entry would have to remain for years out of his patent. Now, it seems quite right that a man should go before a judge and show that he has those qualities of citizenship that entitle him to naturalization, but it does not seem fair that he should be compelled to have reached that stage of literacy which was not compulsory under the law as it stood when he took entry. Consequently, if the only reason why a man cannot get his certificate is his inability to speak French or English, we do not wish to keep him out of his patent, and the effect of this provision is to enable us to give him that patent.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: BIL.L TO CONFIRM THE AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
As far as I know it includes everything the leader of the Opposition asks for. The Acting Prime Minister drew my

attention to the request of the leader of the Opposition and I have had the Department of Justice and the Department of Railways and Canals proceed with the making oi copies of everything that they could find in connection with it. I would like to proceed with the Bill and make some progress. It is for the purpose of correcting two small errors that were made in the schedule to the agreement as presented to Parliament last session. There is a second clause which sufficiently ratifies the agreement that was made last year in addition to the correction of these two errors. The reason I am bringing the Bill before Parliament is this: The Grand Trunk Company noticed that they had omitted to mention one railway in the schedule and they had made a mistake in describing the other.
They made a mistake in not including Vermont and Province Line railway, which is only a small line some three miles long. Another mistake was made by stating in the agreement that the Pembroke Southern Railway Company was controlled by lease, whereas it is controlled by stock ownership majority. In this connection I received the following letter from Mr. W. H. Biggar, *solicitor for the Grand Trunk Railway system.
Montreal, March 17, 1920.. Major G. A. Bell, C.M.G.,
Deputy Minister, Department of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa. Canada.
Dear Sir,-A careful check of the companies enumerated in the first schedule of the agreement between the Company and the Government reveals two slight errors. The Vermont and Province Line, extending from the Canadian boundary to Albrugh Junction, 3.16 miles, is omitted from the list. This line is the property formerly operated in connection with the Canada Atlantic railway and is owned by the Vermont and Province Line Railroad Company, the capital stock of which ($200,000) is now owned by this company. The schedule also shows the Pembroke and Southern Railway Company as controlled by lease, whereas it is controlled through the ownership of a majority of the capital stock of the Pembroke Southern Railway Company.
Tours faithfully.
W. H. Biggar.
Major Bell handed the foregoing letter to me. I then sent for Mr. Kelley, president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and discussed the matter with him. I also discussed it with the Department of Justice, Mr. Kelley being present, and the Department of Justice could not see any other way of correcting these errors in the schedule than by introducing and passing through

Parliament a Bill adding the Vermont and Province Line railway in the schedule and correcting the error so far as ownership of the other line was concerned. If we were of our own motion to make these changes, it would also be necessary to have another meeting of the shareholders of the company to confirm the changes, and that would involve considerable delay. After drawing the attention of Mr. Kelley to this situation he proceeded to Montreal and took the matter up with Mr. Biggar and other legal gentlemen concerned, and afterwards wrote me the following letter:

Montreal, Que., April 7. 1920. The Hon. J. D. Reid, M.D., M.P.,
Minister of Railways and Canals.
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Referring to Mr. Biggar's letter of March 17th last, addressed to the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, calling attention to certain errors in the first schedule to the agreement which has been executed between the Government and the Grand Trunk under [he authority of the Grand Trunk Acquisition Act, 1919, I consider it advisable that the errors in the schedule should be corrected by legislation; and the provisions of the enclosed Bill which has been drafted for that purpose are satisfactory to this company.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) Howard G. Kelley, President.
That is the reason I have introduced this Bill and why I would like to have it passed by Parliament.
The second clause of the agreement is for the purpose of ratifying the corrections of the errors made and dispensing with another meeting of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company o which would otherwise be necessary for the purpose of obtaining their ratification. Of course we ratify the whole agreement under that clause, thus precluding the possibility of any question being raised in the future in connection with this matter. The leader of the Opposition asked for all papers and correspondence in connection with the subject. I have now before me the whole correspondence, covering the period from the time the agreement was completed and forwarded to England to be approved by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and as that correspondence is not very long and explains succinctly the whole situation I will, with the approval of the House read it. The first letter, dated January 22, 1920, was written by myself to Sir George Perley, High Commissioner, London, and is as follows:

Enc. Certified Copy of O.C.
6 copies of agreement, and copy of Act.
January 22, 1920.
Dear Sir George:-
I enclose herewith a certified copy of an Order in Council of the 31st December, ultimo (P.C. 2504), authorizing execution on behalf of His Majesty of the agreement proposed to be entered into with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada under the terms of the Act passed by Parliament at its last session entitled " An Act respecting the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway system." You will observe that this Order in Council provides as follows:
' That he (the Minister of Railways and Canals) be authorized also to deposit with the High Commissioner for Canada in London, England, a number (approximately six) of executed originals of the said agreement, and to instruct the High Commissioner to permit the proper officers of the Grand Trunk to inspect such executed originals at any time, and also to permit such officers to execute on behalf of the Grand Trunk the originals so deposited after ratification of the said agreement by a majority in voting power of the holders of the stock enumerated in the preamble to the said Act present in person, or by proxy, and voting at a special meeting of stock holders, duly called for the purpose of considering such agreement.
That he (the Minister of Railways and Canals) be authorized also to instruct the said High Commissioner upon satisfying himself that the said meeting was duly held, and the said agreement duly ratified and the signing officers duly authorized to execute the said agreement under the seal of the Grand Trunk, and that the said agreement has been duly executed to deliver to the said officers signing the agreement on behalf of the Grand Trunk, or either of them, two executed originals of the said agreement as executed, returning to the minister three originals, as executed, and retaining one executed original for the files of his office for the examination and inspection of all parties concerned.
Six copies of this agreement have been executed on behalf of His Majesty and the same are herewith enclosed in order that the provisions of the Order in Council above quoted may be carried out by you.
For your information, I enclose. herewith a copy of the Act referred to.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd) J. D. Reid.
I again wrote Sir George Perley next day to the following effect:
January 23, 1920.
Dear Sir George:-
Adverting to my letter to you of the 22nd January, 1920, enclosing a certified copy of the Order in Council passed on the 31st December ultimo, under the provisions of the Grand Trunk Railway Acquisition Act, 1919, and also enclosing six executed originals of the Arbitration Agreement to be dealt with under the provisions of the said Order, I omitted to mention that it is expedient that, in acting under the provisions of the Order, you should be advised, in every step taken, by competent legal
authority. For instance, your legal representatives should advise you that the meeting referred to in the Order in Council was duly called and duly held, that the agreement was duly ratified and the signing officers were duly authorized to execute and that the said agreement was duly executed. I would like to suggest that your legal representative, by arrangement with the Grand Trunk, should actually attend the meeting and collaborate with the Grand Trunk authorities in assuring himself that all necessary steps are properly taken.
Parliament has authorized an appropriation out of which all expenditures so occasioned may be defrayed.
You will also be good enough to arrange that the date of the executed originals of the agreement be made concurrent with the execution thereof by the Grand Trunk authorities.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd) J. D. Reid.
The Rt. Hon. Sir George H. Perley,

There is only one other letter. It is from Mr. Kelley asking that this Bill be passed I have already read it. Before going any {further I might explain that when the -agreement was received from England, officers of the Department of Justice and the solicitors who are to act with the Government in connection with this arbitration had the agreement and the correspondence placed before them, the question of the calling ol the meeting being, of course, what they were considering. In England the meeting was called regularly in accordance with the by-laws of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Notices were sent to 70,000 shareholders; but in addition to the sending oi the notices, in order that no question might arise as to the shareholders knowing exactly what was coming before this special meeting, a copy of the proposed agreement was enclosed with the notice to every shareholder to the number of some 70,000. There could, therefore, be no question whatever as to the validity of the meeting in that respect. In Canada there are a few shareholders who would come under this Act, in a cable which I read mentioned the number -and the meeting was. called by inserting a notice in the Canada Gazette. That is the only respect in regard to which the validity of the meeting might be called in question, and, as I understand the matter, the decision of the Deputy Minister of Justice and the other solicitors is that the meeting was regularly called, although a special notice had not been sent to each of these few shareholders in Canada. If it had not been for the two mistakes, we would have proceeded to carry out the agreement in -accordance with the Act passed last session. As, however, we must on account of these mistakes come to Parliament and as it would have to be ratified by another meeting of the shareholders, we decided that it would be better to ratify the agreement as regards these and also the question that had been raised, although in the opinion of the Minister of Justice, that would not be necessary. In order to make the matter final, clause 2 was inserted in the Bill1.

With further reference to your letters of the 22nd and 23rd January last, in connection with the agreement of the Grand Trunk Railway Company-

This is a letter from Sir Charles Russell addressed to W. L. Griffith, Esq., Office of the High Commissioner for Canada:
37 Norfolk Street,
London, W.C., 2, 8th March. 1920-. Dear Sir,-
Grand Trunk Railway Co. of Canada,
We beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 5 th instant enclosing a copy of a cablegram of the same date received by you from the Minister of Justice, Ottawa.
We notice that this cablegram is in practically the same terms as that dated the 4th instant which was received by you from the Minister of Railways and Canals and in addition it asks for our opinion as to whether the meeting which was held was regularly constituted.
With regard to this point, section 7 of the Grand Trunk Railway Acquisition Act, 1919, provides that the meeting is to be a meeting of the holders of the stocks enumerated in the preamble to the Act and the meeting which was called was a meeting of the company at which the Great Western stockholders have apparently no right to attend or vote. In our opinion therefore the meeting which was held was not strictly in accordance with the above-mentioned Act.
At the same .time we think it right to point out that even if notice of the meeting had been given to all the holders of the Great Western debenture stock, and they had power to attend and vote at the meeting, and had in fact all attended and all voted against the resolution, unless they were to be treated as entitled to voting rights far greater than those of any other class of stockholders there would still have been at the meeting, a large majority of votes in favour of the resolution.
As the matter was of considerable importance we thought it well to have the benefit of the advice of counsel and we enclose two copies of his opinion as no doubt you would desire to forward a copy to Canada.
We are obtaining the necessary evidence asked for by the Minister of Railways and Canals in his cablegram of the 4th inst. and in accordance with such cablegram we propose to have the agreements executed by the company^ and hand thetn to the High Commissioner with this evidence so that he may communicate with Canada in order that the Government may be advised as to whether the agreement has been properly ratified. We shall at the same time send the High Commissioner a full report on the matter.
The declaration referred to in Counsel's Opinion will contain the evidence which has been askd for.
Tours faithfully,
(Sgd.) Charles Russell. W. L. Griffith, Esq.,
Office of the High Commissioner for Canada, 19, Victoria Street, S.W. 1.

.This is a letter from Mr. George R. North-cote, giving his opinion as counsel in regard to the matter:
The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.
Opinion.
1,	2 and 3. I have considered this matter and have settled the accompanying draft statutory declaration to be made by the chairman and secretary of the company. The resolution passed at the meeting on the 19th February last is in the form previously approved by me. I am afraid, however, that even if a statutory declaration to the effect of the draft herewith is made the High Commissioner cannot be advised to proceed upon the assumption that the matter is in order until the question referred to below with regard to the sufficiency of the meeting held has been disposed of. It is a question depending largely on the construction of the Grand Trunk Railway Acquisition Act, 1919, and which will I understand and should 1 think be dealt with by the Canadian Government on the advice of its law officers. The question is whether the meeting which was held on the 19th February last was such a meeting as is contemplated by section 7 of the Act, section 7 requires the agreement to be ratified by a majority in voting power of the holders of the stocks enumerated in the preamble to the Act present in person or by proxy at a special general meeting of such stockholders duly called for the purpose of Considering such agreement. The preamble to the Act after setting out the capital and debenture stocks of the company contains a statement to the effect that the debenture stockholders were entitled to certain voting powers at meetings of the shareholders (Sic) of the company. That statement appears however to have been inaccurate since the holders of the 5 per cent Great Western debenture stock have as I understand no rights of attending and voting at meetings of the company. The regulations of the company provide for the convening of ordinary or special general meetings of the company by 14 days' notice advertised in the Canada Gazette but do not, as I understand, provide for meetings of the stockholders as such and the meeting of the 19th February was convened as a meeting of the company by advertisement in the Canada Gazette. I think that if all the stockholders referred to in the preamble to the Act had been entitled to attend and vote at the meeting, it might fairly have been regarded as such a meeting as was required to satisfy section 7 of the Act but inasmuch as the holders of the 5 per cent Great Western debenture stock were not entitled to attend and vote at it, it seems to me open to question whether it can be so regarded although it may be contended that the intention of the legislature was that the ratification of the agreement should be determined by the votes of persons entitled to vote at meetings of the company; and it is further to be observed that, unless the Great Western debenture stockholders were to be treated as entitled to voting rights far greater than those of any other class of stockholder there would still have been at the meeting a large majority of votes in favour of the resolution even if all the Great Western debenture stockholders had voted against it. But, as I have said, the point is in my opinion one to be dealt with by the Government and not to be decided by the High Commissioner on his own responsibility. I do not think section 7 requires separate meet-

ings of the different classes of stockholders to he held, or a majority of each class to be obtained in favour of ratifying the Agreement and in my opinion if the meeting satisfied the section the agreement was duly ratified.
(Sgd.) George R. Northcotb,
2 New Square.
5th March, 1920.
There is another opinion, from Sir Charles Russell, dated March 12, 1920, as follows:
Re the Grand Trunk Railway Company of _	Canada.	.
With reference to the letters of the 22nd and 23rd January which were received by you from the Minister of Railways and Canals enclosing a certified copy of the Order in Council dated the 3'lst December, 1919, together with six copies of the proposed agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada executed by the Minister of Railways and Canals, and a copy of the Grand Trunk Railway Acquisition Act, 1919. we have now given this matter very careful consideration.
The Order in Council dated the 31st December, 1919, authorised the execution on behalf of His Majesty of the agreement proposed to be entered into with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada under the terms of the Act passed by Parliament entitled "An Act respecting the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway System." This order provided as follows:
"That he (the Minister of Railways and . Canals) be authorised also to deposit with the High Commissioner for Canada in London, England, a number (approximately six) of executed originals of the said agreement, and to instruct the High Commissioner to permit the proper officers of the Grand Trunk to inspect such executed originals at any time, and also to permit such officers to execute on behalf of the Grand Trunk the originals, so deposited after ratification of the said agreement by a majority in voting power of the holders of the stock enumerated in the preamble to the said Act present in person, or by proxy, and voting at a special meeting of stockholders duly called for the purpose of considering such agreement. That he (the Minister of Railways and Canals) be authorised also to instruct the said High Commissioner upon satisfying himself that the said meeting was duly held and the said agreement duly ratified and the signing officers duly authorised to execute the said agreement under the seal of the Grand Trunk and that the said agreement has been duly executed to deliver to the said officers signing the agreement on behalf of the Grand Trunk, or either of them, two executed originals of the said agreement, as executed, returning to the minister three originals and retaining one executed (as executed) original for the files of his office for the examination and inspection of all parties concerned." The letter of the 23rd January above referred to stated that in acting under the provisions of the order, you Should be advised in every step taken by competent legal authority, and that your legal representative should advise you that the meeting referred to in the Order in Council was duly called and duly held, that the agreement was duly ratified and the signing officers were duly authorised to execute and that the agreement was duly executed. This letter also suggested that your legal representative by arangement with the Grand Trunk should attend the meeting and collaborate with
the company in assuring himself that all necessary steps were properly taken.
Upon receipt of your instructions we at once placed ourselves in communication with the company and their solicitors, with a view to being satisfied that all necessary formalities had been complied with as regards the proposed meeting. Owing, however, to the limited time at their disposal and to the somewhat complicated nature of the Acts of the company which govern the matter, of which, as you are doubtless aware, there are a great number, they were unable to satisfy us definitely on .all paints before the meeting. The meeting which had been convened was therefore held, and these points were allowed to stand over to be dealt with after the meeting.
The meeting was held on the 19th February and was attended by 'Sir Charles Russell, and as will be seen from the documents sent herewith the agreement was ratified by such meeting.
We enclose the following documents;
(1)	Six parts of the agreement duly executed by ail parties.
(2)	Statutory declaration, of Sir Alfred W. Smithers and Mr. Henry Hilton Norman, the chairman and secretary of the company respectively, verifying the facts, together with the following, exhibits therein referred to:
(a)	A cutting from the Canada Gazette of the 31st January, 1920, containing the notice convening the meeting being Exhibit "A."
(b)	The circular and draft of the agreement which was sent to the stockholders being Exhibit "B."
In acordance with the cablegrams of the 4th March received by you from the Minister of Railways and Canals, and the 5th March from the Minister of Justice, we have had the agreement executed by the company, and have also obtained the above-mentioned statutory declaration as evidence of the facts.
We are afraid however that notwithstanding this declaration we are unable to advise you to proceed upon the assumption that the matter is in order until the question referred to below with regard to the sufficiency of the meeting held has been disposed of. It is a question depending largely on the construction of the Grand Trunk Railway Acquisition Act 1919, and which will we understand and should we think be dealt with by the Canadian Government on the advice of its law officers.
The question is whether the meeting which was held on the 19th February last was such a meeting as is contemplated by Section 7 of the Act.
Section 7 requires the agreement to be ratified by a majority in voting power of the holders of the stocks enumerated in the preamble to the Act present in person or by proxy at a special general meeting of such stockholders duly called for the purpose of considering such agreement. The preamble to the Act after setting out the capital and debenture stocks of the company contains a statement to the effect that the debenture stockholders were entitled to certain voting powers at meetings of the shareholders (sic) of the company. That statement appears however to have been inaccurate since the holders of the five per cent Great Western Debenture Stock have as we understand no rights of attending and voting at meetings of the company. The regulations of the company provide for the convening of ordinary or special general meetings of the company by fourteen days notice advertised in the Canada Gazette, but do not as we understand, provide for

meetings of the stockholders as such; and the meeting of the 19th February was convened as a meeting of the company by advertisement in the Canada Gazette. We think that if all the stockholders referred to in the preamble to the Act had been entitled to attend and vote at the meeting, it might fairly have been regarded as such a meeting as was required to satisfy section 7 of the said Act. but inasmuch as the holders of the five per cent Great Western Debenture Stock were not entitled to attend and vote at it, it seems to us open to question whether it can be so regarded although it may be* contended that the intention of the legislature was that the ratification of the agreement should be determined by the votes of persons entitled to vote at meetings of the company ; and it is further to be observed that, unless the 6reat Western Debenture Stockholders were to be 'treated as entitled to voting rights far greater than those of any other class of stockholders, there would still have been at the meeting a large majority of votes in favour of the resolution even if all the Great Western Debenture Stockholders had voted against it, but as we have said, the point is in our opinion one to be dealt with by the Government and not to be decided by you on your own responsibility.	t
We do not think section 7 requires separate meetings of the different classes of stockholders to be held or a majority of each class to be obtained in favour of ratifying the agreement and in our opinion if the meeting satisfied the section the agreement was duly ratified.
We have discussed the matter fully with counsel and you will see from the copy of his opinion which we have furnished to you that he confirms the above view.
We think that with a view to saving time it would be advisable that you should at once cable to the minister of Railways giving him full particulars and asking whether the Government are now satisfied as to the meeting and whether you may now hand the company their parts of the agreement.
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) Charles RXtssell.
The Hon. Sir George H. Perley, K.C.M.G.,
High Commissioner for Canada, [DOT]
19 Victoria street,
Westminster, S.W.

Dear Mr. Griffith:
Re Grand Trunk Railway.
I am in receipt of Sir George Perley's letter of the 15th instant giving me a copy of a further cablegram received from the Canadian Minister of Justice and also enclosing copies of the following cablegrams:-
5th March. Minister of Justice to the High commissioner.
12th March. The High Commissioner to the Minister of Justice.
12th March. The High Commissioner to the Minister of Railways and Canals.
With regard to the points raised in your letter:-[DOT]

1.	You will notice that clause 15 of the Statutory Declaration which was made by the chairman and secretary contains a complete copy of the resolution ratifying the agreement and states that it was proposed and carried by a large majority. I however enclose a separate copy of the resolution certified by the chairman.
2.	With regard to the grounds justifying the omission to notify the Great Western stockholders, clause 12 of thd declaration states that although the stockholders are not entitled as of right to receive personal notices of general meetings of the company it has been the practice for many years past, to send each stockholder including the five per cent Great Western stockholders on the company's London Register, copy of the notice of every meeting; that copies of the notices are usually posted about eight days before the meeting and copies are not sent to stockholders on the Canadian Register as it would be useless to do so as they would not be received in time for the stockholders to act upon them at the meetings. This disposes of the point as to why notice was not given to the Great Western stockholders in Canada. I have however, received from the solicitors of the company further letters of the 16th and 17th instant dealing with the matter and setting out these reasons at length and I enclose copies of them herewith.
Clause 13 of the declaration sets out that notice was given to the holders of the five per cent Great Western stock in the English register.
3.	With regard to the agreement which has been executed I think possibly it would be the best course if the High Commissioner were to send three parts of it to Canada together with the declaration and other evidence and ask the Minister of Railways and Canals if he is satisfied with regard to the meeting, to cable with instructions to hand two parts to the company and to retain the other in the custody of the High Commissioner as provided by the Order in Council.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd.) Charles Russell.
W. L. Griffith, Esq.,
19 Victoria Street, S.W.X.
This is all the correspondence in connection with the matter, but if it is thought necessary I shall read the declarations. If the Department of Justice had considered that there was any doubt in regard to the validity o'f the meeting the matter could have been justified without recourse to the House simply by convening another meeting of the shareholders. But, as I have pointed out, in the opinion of the Department of Justice there was no necessity for bringing the question before Parliament but for the two errors; and as we have to come to the House to complete-the schedule, we shall at the same time obtain ratification of the agreement as passed by the shareholders. As I said at the outset, there is no question about the meeting so far as the shareholders in England are concerned.

In the correspondence' which the minister has read, reference is made to some Orders in Council that were

apparently transmitted with instructions from the Government seemingly defining the procedure to be followed. I do not know if the minister has read those Orders in Council. If not, are they available for the information of the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In the very first letter in which I enclosed the agreement I said:
" You will observe that this Order in Council provides as follows"; and then I recited the provisions of the Order in Council. I take it for granted that the Order in Council has been laid upon the Table, but whether it has been or not I may just as well read the clause again:
That he (the Minister of Railways and Canals) be authorized also to deposit with the High Commissioner for Canada in London, England, a number (approximately six) of executed originals of the said agreement, and to instruct the High Commissioner to permit the proper officers of the Grand Trunk to inspect such executed originals at any time, and also to permit such officers to execute on behalf of the Grand Trunk the originals, so deposited after ratification of the said agreement by a majority in voting power of the holders of the stock enumerated in the preamble to the said Act present in person, or by proxy, and voting at a special meeting of stockholders duly called for the purpose of considering such agreement. That he (the Minister of Railways and Canals) be authorized also to instruct the said High Commissioner upon satisfying himself that the said meeting was duly held and the said agreement duly ratified and the signing officers duly authorized to execute the said agreement under the seal of the Grand Trunk and that the said agreement has been duly executed to deliver to the said officers signing the agreement on behalf of the Grand Trunk, or either of them, two executed originals of the said agreement, as executed, returning to the Minister three originals and retaining one executed (as executed) original for the files of his office for the examination and inspection of all parties concerned.
Is that the only Order in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is the only Order in Council in connection with the whole matter.

The minister referred to an opinion expressed by the Department of Justice on the matter in regard to which some question was raised in the correspondence. Is that opinion of the department in writing?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No. When we were
discussing the two errors and the necessity for this Bill, the whole question came up as to the validity of the meeting, and the whole correspondence was discussed with the Deputy Minister of Justice, the opinion being expressed that the meeting was legal and had been called in accordance with the 80
terms of the Grand Trunk Act. There would, therefore, have been no necessity for us to come back to the House had it not been for the errors. There was some doubt on the part of the solicitors in England, but they referred the matter to the Government of Canada for an opinion from the Department of Justice. As we are compelled to come before Parliament we are taking the precaution to ratify the agreement reached at the meeting, and no one is injured because the 70,000 shareholders in England undoubtedly received sufficient notice. They got a notice calling the meeting, together with a copy of the agreement, and there was a very large majority in favour of the carrying out of that agreement If we called another meeting it would probably take two or three months before we could get them together and give the notice that would be necessary to ratify the agreement so that there could be no possible doubt. I have the statutory declaration here from Sir Alfred Smithers certifying to the resolution that was passed at the general meeting:
The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.
.	Resolution.
Passed at a special general meeting of the company held at the Cannon Street Hotel, Cannon street, London, E.C., on Thursday the 19th, February 1920 at twelve o'clock noon.
Resolved, that the agreement between His Majesty the King, represented by the Minister of Railways and Canals of Canada, acting under the authority of an Order in Council dated 31st December, 1919 and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada the draft of which is now submitted to this meeting, be and the same is hereby approved and ratified, and that Sir Alfred Waldron Smithers, M.P., chairman of the Board of Directors, and Henry Hilton Norman secretary of the company, be and they are hereby authorized on behhif of the company to sign the said agreement and afix the corporate seal of the company thereto.
I certify the above to be a true copy.
(Sgd.) Alfred W. Smithers,
Chairman.
I have a letter adreased to Charles Russell & Company by Batten & Company which I would like to read:
Copy.
13, Victoria Street, Westminster, S.W.I.,
16th March, 1920. Messrs. Charles Russell & Co.
Grand Trunk.
Dear Sirs,-To prevent any possibility of misunderstanding we think it is better to write you at length in confirmation of what we have already told you verbally.
We are of opinion, and this is confirmed by our counsel, that the only notice necessary for the purpose of calling the meeting required to ratify the agreement with the company was the notice published in the " Canada Gazette." It is recognized we think by all parties thar

If the Department of
Justice is of opinion that the meeting was regular, and if counsel for the Grand Trunk is also of the opinion that the meeting was regular why should the Bill be introduced?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I explained that at the outset. We are introducing the Bill to correct two errors that were made. One is that a railway has been left out altogether. We would have to introduce a Bill to correct that error and we would also have to introduce a Bill to correct the mistake in reference to the other railway which is described as a leasehold instead of a road controlled

by majority stock ownership. We would also have to have a meeting of the Grand Trunk for the purpose of ratifying that even if we had gone on with our regular agreement. By this Bill we are ratifying the agreement as a whole as well. We have the opinion of the Grand Trunk solicitors in England that without doubt the meeting had been regularly called. We have also the opinion of Sir Charles Russell and two others. They raised a question of doubt, but they say it is a matter that should be decided by the Department of Justice, or by the law officers of the Government, in Ottawa.
If I understand the minister rightly, the agreement could not be completed unless this thing is adopted by Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Oh, no.	[DOT]
If this Bill is 'not adopted by Parliament the Government will have to see that a new meeting of the shareholders is called?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No, I do not go that far. So far as the agreement passed last session is concerned the law officers are of the opinion that that agreement is legal; that as the meeting was called we could proceed now without any further meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders and act under that agreement; but after going on with the agreement and acting on it, we would have to come to Parliament to get these two mistakes corrected. .Now as we have to come to Parliament to make the two corrections, the Government feel that it is just as well to clear up any possible doubt that has been raised in connection -with the possibility of the meeting in question not having been legally called. I think that is a fair answer to the hon. gentleman.

When this Bill, as it now reads, has been adopted will it be possible for a shareholder of the Grand Trunk who thinks that his interests have not been properly protected to protest before any court of justice and secure that better protection?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Out of all the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway only two of them could raise any question about the agreement, and so far as the Department of Justice is concerned-
How many shares would they possess?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: Those shareholders would be debarred from any recourse before any tribunal?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Not the owners of the $100,000 but only two, because of the eight referred to, six did receive notice in the regular way.
In addition there are two or three declarations which, if I read them, would complete all the documents pertaining to this matter so far as I am aware. There is first of all a notice of the meeting signed by Sir Alfred Wilfred Smithers and Henry Hilton Norman which was published in the Canada Gazette:
Canada Gazette, Ottawa, January 31, 1920.

This is the exhibit marked " A " referred to in the statutory declaration of Sir Alfred Waldron Smithers and Henry Hilton Norman made before me this 12th day of March, 1920.
(Sgd.) Arthuh F. Greenwood.
A Commissioner for Oaths.

speechtext:
Notice is hereby given that a special general meeting of the Grand Trunk- Railway Company of Canada will be held at the Cannon Street Hotel. Cannon street, London. E.C.. on Thursday, the 19th February, 1920, at twelve o'clock noon precisely, for the purpose of considering, and if approved, of ratifying an agreement between His Maiesty the King, represented by the Minister of Railways and Canals of Canada, of the first part, and the company, of the second part, the draft of which agreement will be submitted to the meeting.
By order,
Sir Alfred W. Smithers,
1	Chairman.

Secretary.

That is the notice that was published in the Canada Gazette and which the law officers of the Grown think was sufficient notice for those shareholders in Canada. As I have said there is only a possibility of two shareholders raising a question of doubt.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext: Was the document published in the Canada Gazette?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK RAILWAY COMPANY OF CANADA.
speechtext:
Yes. I will now read a copy of a circular which was distributed by the Directors of the Grand Trunk among the shareholders:

The present railway conditions are worldwide ; they are caused by the effects of the war; if the railways are to be maintained and if new capital is to be found for new extensions, the railways must be placed on a paying basis. When the Government of Canada becomes the owner of a great railway system, such as it will have when it acquires the Grand Trunk it can speedily bring about such a readjustment of rates as will permit a fair return on the capital involved. The whole cause of the present difficulty of the Grand Trunk is its being required to carry on an .ever increasing business under the present phenomenal operating costs without a corresponding increase in rates, and that condition cannot be altered until the Railway Commission allow an adequate increase of rates.
It is under these circumstances, and after n. long and anxious consideration, that the Board unhesitatingly advise the Proprietors to accept the agreement, and vote for the same either in person at the General Meeting or by signing the enclosed Form of Proxy and returning it forthwith to the Secretary.
The Committee, whose names are given above, appointed to confer with the Directors, unanimously join with the Board in recommending the Proprietors to accept the agreement.
On behalf of the Board,

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Chairman.
A copy of the agreement is attached. That is a copy of the notice that was sent to the 70,000 shareholders in England
Was that circular sent to the shareholders of the Vermont and Province Line Railroad Company, and of the Pembroke Southern Railway Company, and to the holders of the Great Western debenture stocks?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: Is there any thing to show how this group of eight voted, or how the two voted?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There is no record of that. The affidavits show that there was no protest from them in any shape or form. This question of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk was so much discussed in the press that I am satisfied these shareholders would know that the meeting was being held. At all events, they are in a much better position to-day, because whereas their stock was guaranteed only by the Grand Trunk it is now guaranteed by the Dominion of -Canada, so instead of being injured they are better off.
What was the date of the declaration which the minister just read?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
March 12, 1920. Even up till that date there had been no protest of any kind from any of these eight shareholders who did not receive notice. I have now brought all the information down. I asked the Deputy Minister of Justice to send me a copy of every document he had in the Justice Department, and the file I have read comes f om that department. I want to repeat that if we were to have the shareholders of the Grand Trunk called to-

gether again to ratify these two errors and the agreement as a whole, it would mean a further two or three month's delay. I am exceedingly anxious, and so of course are the Grand Trunk officials who are operating the railway, and the officials of the Canadian National Railway, that we should get the systems linked up as soon as possible so that we can effect economies. Immediately the agreement is ratified, we shall- be able to appoint the Committee of Management, who will try and effect all economies possible, and there is no doubt that the economies can be effected. To give an instance, in the city of -Ottawa we have two very expensive offices selling tickets, one for the Grand Trunk, and the other for the Canadian National. There is no reason, so far as I can see, why we should not dispense with one office at once, and the same is true of other parts of Canada.
Why do-es not the minister do in Ottawa Wh-ait was done in Quebec, close up the Grand Trunk office?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is exactly what I was suggesting.
That has already been done in Quebec.
They are progressive in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We cannot close the Grand Trunk office until we have appointed the Committee of Management.
The Quebec office has been closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I do not know why it has been done. I shall be pleased when we are in committee to give all information that may be -asked for, and I trust hon. members will -see their way clear to ratify the agreement at the earliest possible moment.
In what way does the minister think the people of Canada would suffer if this agreement were not carried into effect at once?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Until it is carried into effect we cannot get the railways working together. I am advised both by Mr. Kelley, of the Grand Trunk, and by Mr. Hanna and his officials, that once 'the agreement is ratified they are prepared to sit down and make plans for effecting economies, in operation very 1-aTgely, as well as for making the operation much easier than at present. As we have to get these two small errors I have spoken of rectified, I feel that although 'the law officers do not think there

is any question as to the validity of the agreement, it is better that we should settle all doubts that may exist by passing this legislation. There is no complaint, and there can be no complaint, from other than two out of the whole list of shareholders.

Touching the question of offices to which the minister has referred, there is in London, in Trafalgar Square, a very fine office of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I take it for granted that that would be included in the property we would acquire.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

The question often arises as to the looaJtion of offices in London for Canada. There is no finer location in London than that of this office in Trafalgar Square, and when we are in committee perhaps the minister would be prepared to tell us what is the nature of the accommodation there, and whether it would serve the purposes of a general office.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In my memory serves me right, this office is part of the Grand Trunk property and will become the property oif the Government. The Canadian Northern also have offices and officials in London, although perhaps the property does ndt amount to much. There is another case where an amalgamation of offices might be effected.
- Mr. CANNON: As long as this agreement is not put into force this country is not responsible for the liabilities or the administration of the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is right, but the position the Government takes is that once the agreement is ratified we must proceed with it.
Would that not explain somewhat the eagerness of the Grand Trunk people to have the Bill put through?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Personally, I am just as anxious as the Grand Trunk to get the matter cleared up, because if we are going to take over the Grand Trunk we should try to get economies under way at the earliest moment. Every member will agree that, if the agreement is to be carried out, the sooner steps are taken in the matter the better. It is unprofitable and unsatisfactory to have two railways paralleling each other, and I think it is well that we should proceed as quickly as possible with this Bill. When we are in committee I shall
be glad to furnish any further information that may be desired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister has given us a two-fold reason for the introduction of this Bill. He has said in the first place that its purpose is to correct two errors that appear in the agreement which the Government has drawn, and which has been signed between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The other purpose of the Bill is to have this Parliament ratify the agreement in toto. I should like to point out to the Government that at the last session of Parliament the Opposition urged very strongly a course of action which, had it been adopted, would have avoided altogether the two-fold necessity which the minister finds himself under at the moment. The Government would not have been obliged to come to-day and confess, as it has, errors in its management of public affairs, and Parliament would not have been obliged to spend further time and to incur further expenditures in connection with this legislation. Hon. members will recall that my hon. friend from Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) at the last session urged a course which he considered necessary in order to obviate just such errors as those that have been pointed out to-day. May I draw the attention of the House to an amendment which was moved by my hon. friend at that time? I shall not read the whole of the amendment, but I may quote that part of it which is of considerable interest just now. In the Journals of the House of Tuesday, November 4, 1919, will be found the amendment moved by the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne, in which the following appears:
That the information in possession of the House is insufficient to enable the House and the people to fully understand the complicated affairs of the Grand Trunk Railway system.
Then there follows this clause:
That the House is of opinion that before taking further action towards the acquisition of the railways referred to, the Government should appoint a commission composed of persons of recognized ability and experience in railway management, railway finance and railway accounting to make a full inquiry into all the affairs of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and its subsidiary companies, their assets and liabilities, the condition of the railway lines and their equipment, the physical value of the properties, the sums required to put them into an efficient condition, their estimated earning powers, and generally into all matters in any way relating to the affairs of the companies herein referred to, and to make a full report thereon for the information of Parliament.

At that time the Government resolutely refused to accept either the amendments or the suggestion that came from this side. To-day, however, we have one consequence at least of the consequence of that refusal." We find that two errors have crept into the agreement, and we have no guarantee, Mr. Speaker, that other errors may not also have occurred. In fact, there is reasonable ground for the supposition, judging by the correspondence read by the minister, that a great many of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway company are entirely dissatisfied with the meeting that was held and the procedure adopted^ a dissatisfaction no doubt due in part to the lack of that full information which would have been disclosed had the course suggested by this side of the House been followed. As I said the other day when the minister brought in this measure, we have no desire on this side to delay in any way any legislation of urgent public importance, but this Bill as introduced goes very much further than the simple question of correcting the two errors which the minister says constitute the main, and in fact, the only object of this legislation. Let me say at once that if by the correction of these two errors we can extricate the Government from the difficulty into which it has brought itself, and provided the minister will agree to confine the scope of the Bill to that purpose, I think we can undertake to pass the measure to-day. I see no reason whatever why we should not agree to the changes which the minister seeks to bring about so far as these particular errors are concerned, and to give any measure of ratification that may be necessary in connection with these errors. But when the minister asks us to [DOT]do more than that, when he demands the ratification of the whole agreement, then he opens up a pretty broad field, and Parliament is put in a position in which it assumes very large responsibilities if' it should take that particular step at 'this time.
I may point out in this connection that at the last session of Parliament I introduced an amendment to the Grand Trunk Railway Bill, an amendment which, had it been adopted, would have covered all that the minister is now asking, even in the larger way of ratification. The proposed amendment will be found at page 155 of the Journals of the House of last session as follows:	[DOT]
Mr. King moved in amendment thereto:-
That this Bill be not now read a Third time but that it be re-committed to a Committee of the "Whole House with instructions to amend 
same, by adding to Section 2 the following: " The agreement herein shall be submitted to and be subject to ratification by the Parliament of Canada."
Yet, every hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, when we of the Opposition introduced the foregoing amendment at the last session of Parliament, voted the proposal down. It is not our fault that the Government finds it necessary to come to Parliament for ratification of the agreement. At that time we were asking that this very step should be taken.
Let me draw the attention of the House to the invidious position in which Parliament finds itself in this matter of ratification. When the measure was under discussion last session, had the course suggested in this amendment been adopted, Parliament would have had the same opportunity of considering this agreement that was afforded the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company when the agreement between them and the Government was submitted to them for their approval. We pointed out then in most emphatic language that the Government was granting to the shareholders in Great Britain a privilege which they 'were denying the representatives of the people of Canada in Parliament, and I desire to emphasize that this House, in being asked to ratify the agreement at the present time, is not accorded the same privilege and consideration that was accorded the shareholders of the Grank Trunk Company in Great Britain.
I see the Minister of Justice prepared to start up and point out that at least we are now getting a chance to ratify but I think he will see the difference I have in mind, as soon as I have an opportunity of explaining it.
The agreement between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company was signed on the 8th March of this year.
It was submitted to the shareholders, and to the debenture stockholders at London for approval on the 19th day of February, 1920. When the shareholders" of the Grand Trunk had this agreement before them it had not been signed by either the Government or the *shareholders. If there were errors such as have been pointed out to us to-day existing in the agreement at that time the shareholders had an opportunity of bringing them to the attention of the Government if they noticed them. On their being pointed out, the shareholders would have been at liberty, if they had so desired, to raise, any question in regard to these features of the agreement before the agreement was

signed. But that is wholly different from the position in which Parliament is placed because Parliament is being asked to ratify this contract which has already been signed by the shareholders and by the Government.
I venture to say that the Government will not permit us to open up the subject matter of the contract for discussion and that they will be unwilling to accept an amendment of the contract in any particular except as to the point in which they have asked Parliament to amend.
The function of Parliament, in so far as this agreement is concerned, is not that of a deliberative assembly considering the wisdom of a particular clause in the contract; Parliament's function is reduced to a simple registration of approval of the action of the Government. Parliament should not be placed in that position. Two or three times during this session I have drawn the attention of the Government to the fact that in 'connection with important matters which they have brought before the House involving the expenditure of public money, action had already been taken upon contracts by Order in Council, and Parliament has not had an opportunity of doing other than registering a'protest against such procedure. Unless the Government is prepared to open up this whole contract and allow the House to make such changes as may be necessary and advisable in the public interest, we should not now be asked simply to ratify the whole agreement when it has been signed by both parties. If we cannot, as the people's representatives in this House be given the same rights and privileges as were given to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk railway in Great Britain I prefer not to have Parliament put in the position of degrading its function as a deliberative assembly to that of a mere registering office for Orders in Council.
What I would suggest to the minister is that if the purpose is, as he said, simply to correct these errors the title of his Bill ought to be not " an Act to confirm the agreement," but an " Act to correct certain errors in the agreement " between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Let him undertake to make that change and we on this side will take no exception to the passing of that particular phase of the Bill. But we will take very strong exception to being forced to appear to be doing one thing when in reality we are doing another, and obliged to give sanction to a transaction the details of which we have had no opportunity to criticise.
It may perhaps be, as the minister himself has told us-and he emphasized it again to-day-that there was no necessity for the ratification feature of the Bill other than in respect to the particular errors to which I have referred. If ratification is needless it is meaningless to ask for it. I do not think Sir that Parliament should be invited by the Government to spend its time on needless or meaningless legislation.
There is this further point; that in the correspondence which the minister has read to the House this afternoon there is a good deal that ought to be carefully considered before we proceed with the further discussion of this measure. The minister told us there were only two or three pages of correspondence. He read for nearly three hours and one would think his one or two pages had expanded into one or two hundred pages. Under the circumstances I would ask my hon. friend not to press the second reading of the Bill until we have had an opportunity of examining more closely the significance of some of the statements made in the correspondence which he has brought down and which call somewhat in question the validity of the meeting of stockholders called to deal with this matter.

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I wish to' comply with the request at once. I do not want to insist on going on with the Bill if the hon. gentleman wishes to look over the correspondence and study it more closely. I suppose there would be no objection to proceeding tomorrow?

speechtext:

therefore move that the debate be adjourned.

Will the correspondence
be printed in Hansard?

speechtext: Yes.
The members will have it to-morrow at twelve o'clock?

speechtext: At ten o'clock.
