speechtext: House again in committee on Bill No. 28 respecting Maple Products.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this Bill was
last before the committee clause 2 had been amended by adding after the figure " 3 " in the sixteenth line of the Bill the words " except with the consent of the Minister of Health."	.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When the Bill was previously in committee some discussion took place in reference to the form of clause 2, and various suggestions were made as to its amendment. Since the discussion I have had the opportunity of giving some further consideration to the clause and I would now suggest that it be amended by striking out the words " or which is composed partly of maple sugar or maple syrup and "
What is the object of this amendment?	.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To make clear the meaning of the section, which I take to be that no article resembling or being an imitation of maple syrup or maple sugar and which is not pure maple sugar or maple syrup may be sold as such.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Coming to subsection 3, when it was before the committee I submitted an amendment which, at the time, was not satisfactory to myself nor to the committee. After giving the matter further consideration I would suggest that the words inserted be struck out and that the clause be amended in this way: Insert in the nineteenth line the words " resembling or being an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup;" and insert in the twentieth line before the word " article " the word '' such."
Will the minister kindly read the clause as it will then stand.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The clause as amended
will read:
The word maple shall not be used either alone or In combination with any word or words or letter or letters, on the label or other mark, illustration or device on a package containing any article of food, resembling or being an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup, or on any such article of food itself, which is not pure maple sugar or pure maple syrup, and any article of food labelled or marked in violation of this subsection shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of the Pood and Drugs Act. 1920.
Members of the committee will see that the effect of the amendment is to limit the exclusive use of the word " maple " to articles of food resembling or being an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup.
It will not interfere in any way with companies having the name " maple "?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, it will make the
meaning of the section clear. It does not interfere with the use of the word " maple " on any other article of food than the articles mentioned.
It would not disqualify the member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) either?

There is an article of
food which is sold as maple butter. Would the sale of that article be prevented?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, the section would
not prevent the sale of maple butter unless it was made up in a way to resemble or imitate maple syrup. I do not know whether maple butter is made up in a way to resemble maple syrup or not. If it were then, the use of the word " maple " would be forbidden under this clause.
Supposing it were of the same colour?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the use of the expression "maple leaf" be permitted in connection with the manufacture or sale of biscuits?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That would not be prohibited by the change in the section. Hon. members will see that the effect of the change is to limit the right to claim the exclusive use of the word " maple " to food products resembling or being an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It was intimated that an officer of the Department of Health visited a factory in which they were manufacturing " Maple Leaf " biscuits and

protested against the continuation of the manufacture as a violation of the old Act. Would the minister consider that such action was proper and in accordance with the provisions of the Act as it formerly stood?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was proper and in accordance with the provisions of the Act as it stood, and those interested in the business have called on the department to enforce the law as against those using the word " maple " in connection with food products that are not of the character of maple sugar or maple syrup. The Government does not feel that such a monopoly in the use of the word " maple " is justified in the public interest and that those who are manufacturing food products which have no resemblance to maple sugar or maple syrup should not be debarred the use of the general word " maple " which is so characteristic of Canada.

Would the section interefer with the manufacture and sale of " Crescent Mapleine "? The advertisement for this product declares that " it is a delicious flavouring for syrups, cakes, candies, bon-bons, ice-cream, frostings, etc." The statement is made that it " contains no maple sugar, syrup nor sap, but produces a taste similar to a maple."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not knowing the character of the product I cannot undertake to express an opinion on the interpretation of the law as applied to that particular product. The courts would have to determine whether the product came within the section or not.

I wish to call the attention of the minister to a case that happened in my county: A gentleman applied to the Trade Department for a patent to manufacture a certain syrup which was called, jf I. remember correctly, "Sucre de fresne." He obtained permission from the department !to put this kind of syrup on the market. Later it was seized by the Department of Public Health, and there has been no redress, although the department has been communicated with on the subject several times. Will these amendments put an end to such conflicts between the two departments, so that a man will know whether he has a right 'to put on the market a product of that kind? .

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No man might put on the market a product in violation of the law ,as it stood, and the law as it stood prohibited the putting on the market of the product my hon. friend has mentioned.
The officers of the department were but enforcing the law as it stood. I have some knowledge of that case; it was drawn to my attention. But I have already intimated that the law as it stood was too broad in its terms; that it is no't right to give a monopoly of the use of the word "maple" to producers of maple syrup - ot maple sugar; that other people have the right to use the word so long as they do not use it in connection with a food pro-duot that resembles or is an imitation of maple syrup or maple sugar.
Does this clause cover other maple products, such as maple candy, maple molasses and maple cream?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will not prohibit the use of the word "maple" in 'connection with any product that does not resemble or is not an imitation of maple, syrup or maple sugar.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move to add as section 3 of the Bill the following:
Every person who violates the provisions of subsection (1) of section 2 of this Act shall be guilty of an offence and shall for the first offence be liable upon summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $200 and costs and not less than $50 and costs, or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding three months, or to both fine and imprisonment, and for each subsequent offence to a fine not exceeding $50-0 and costs and less than $50 and costs, or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding six months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
This section is taken from the old Adulteration Act and is necessary in order to make this Bill effective.

Many persons may commit an offense against this law without full knowledge of its provisions. I suggest, therefore, that the minimum fine for the first offence be not stated, but be left to the judgment of the magistrate who deals with the case.	.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the committee think it desirable I have no objection to reducing the amount of the minimum fine for the first offence, but some amount should be stated. I am not aware that any hardship has arisen under the existing law. The men interested in having this law enforced are the producers of maple syrup and maple sugar, who desire to protect the pure product against the .adulterated product which is sold as pure maple syiup or pure maple sugar. I think that the provision is quite all right as it is, but if the committee desire

to have the minimum fine reduced to $10, I have no objection.
I suggest, then, that it be made $10.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I agree that the minimum fine for first offence shall be $10 instead of $50.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
New section 3 as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move that the following be added as section 4 of the Bill:
4. Every person who violates any of the provisions of subsections (2) and (3) of said sections shall be guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction to the penalties prescribed by section 16 of "The Food and Drugs Act, 1920".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
On the title:

I was not in the House when section 3 was adopted. If it has been carried as it appears in the Bill, I think it works a hardship which was not intended, and I should like the privilege of making a few remarks in that Tegard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure that the committee will allow the hon. member to make an inquiry concerning the clause. The clause cannot be re-opened after it has been adopted.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend's apprehension will be removed, I think, when I tell him that the clause has been amended in committee by inserting in the 19th line, after the word "food," the words "resembling or being an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup."
I am satisfied with that explanation; it covers axactly the point which I had ill mind.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall the Bill be read the third time?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the Bill has been amended in committee the third reading can only take place at this time by unanimous consent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in Committee on Bill No. 27, respecting food and drugs.-Hon. Mr. Rowell-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
TMr. Rowell.]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the Bill was last before the committee several clauses had been adopted; others had been allowed to stand. The first clause which had been allowed to stand was clause 5.
On section 5-Food, when deemed to be misbranded:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This clause stood in order that I might consider certain suggestions made by members of the committee in connection with different paragraphs. I have now had an opportunity of giving them consideration with the officers of the department, and I wish to move some amendments which, I think, would remove any objections which have been raised and which would at the same time carry out the full object sought by the provisions of this clause. Hon. members will recall that paragraph (a) read:
Food shall be deemed to be misbranded within the meaning* of this Act.-
(a) if it is an imitation of the article under whose name it is sold or offered for sale and if it is not clearly and explicitly described as an imitation.
I would move to substitute for paragraph (a) the following:
If it is an imitation of or substitute for or resembles, in a manner likely to deceive, another article of food under the name of which it is exposed or offered for sale, and is not plainly and conspicuously labelled so as to indicate its true character.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) made, in reference to paragraph (c), a suggestion, the substance of which might well be adopted. I would move that the following be substituted for paragraph (c):
If it is sold or offered for sale by a name which does not belong to it.
Does that mean that every article offered for sale will have a name registered?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
I think paragraph (c), as it originally read, was clearer. The amendment suggested by the minister might be construed as meaning that every article offered for sale must have a name of its own.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Paragraph (c) has already been amended to read as follows:
If it is sold or offered for sale hy a name other than that which belongs to such article.

I would suggest that we come back to the wording of the paragraph as

printed in the Bill, because, otherwise, the paragraph means that every article offered for sale must have a name that belongs to it.

According to my memorandum some one suggested the other night that the words "of the same kind'' should be added, so that the paragraph would read:.
If it is sold or offered for sale by a name which belongs to another article of the same kind.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am quite content to
leave it in the form in which it was originally drafted or to accept the suggestion of the leader of the Opposition, which I moved, in substance, to-night. I do not think difficulty would arise in either case; in the practical working out of the law, either form would be satisfactory.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am quite content to take either form.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then, perhaps, we had
better leave it as it was originally in the Bill.

Would not the minister
add the words "of the same kind" so as to make the paragraph more explicit?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There might be something slightly different. A name might be used for the purpose of misleading on something that was nearly akin, but not exactly of the same kind. I prefer to leave the paragraph as it stands.

I find myself returning to a difficulty which arose when the matter was up before. What constitutes "to belong to"? Each of these articles claims a certain name and in neither case is it a registered trade-mark. How do you prove that it belongs to one and not to the other? There is a difficulty in establishing that it belongs to either unless it is a trade-mark.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My recollection is that this is the same paragraph as has been in the Act for some years; I do not think this particular one has been changed, and if no difficulty has arisen so far, we might, perhaps, retain it.
Amendment withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The paragraph will stand as originally drafted. I desire to suggest two or three amendments in reference to paragraph (f) which was thq. one on which most discussion took place. I move that paragraph (f) be amended by inserting in the eighteenth line of section 5, after the word "stated," the words "within limits of variability to be fixed by regulations." It
has been pointed out to me by men engaged in the trade that it is not always possible to have the exact weight or the exact size; *that some slight limits Of variability must be permitted.- Therefore, this change has been suggested, and I think it will be an improvement in the practical working of the clause.

Do I understand that this paragraph would apply, for instance, to a farmer who goes to the city to sell his goods to a grocer? Would he have to put in different packages everything that he brings from the country to the city?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. My hon. friend will see that it must be "in package form, sealed by the manufacturer or producer." If the goods are sold in a sealed package where the contents are not open to inspection, and the package bears his name and address, the'contents of the package must be clearly and correctly stated upon the outside of the package.
Does the word "producer" cover a farmer?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it would cover any [DOT] man who sold his goods in package form, ana sealed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I desire to move to add the following to this clause:
Provided that this subsection shall not apply to packages the weight of which including the package and contents is under two ounces.
It has been pointed out to me by manufacturers that it is very difficult to be absolutely accurate as to the exact weight of packages of very small size. As a business proposition, there are difficulties in the way of applying this provision to very small packages.

The previous line refers to "regulations," but it does not say by whom they are to be made. In fact, there are two parties making regulations later on in the Bill. The general statement, "by regulations" is rather vague. It would be better, I think, to say, "by regulations as hereinafter provided."
Would a farmer putting up butter in a pound package be obliged to put his name on each package?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
He is a producer.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend has not read the clause carefully. It

only applies if certain conditions exist; first, if it is in package form, secondly, if it is sealed by the manufacturer or producer, and third, if it bears his name and address. If he puts it up in a sealed package bearing his name and address he must go a step further and clearly state the contents and weight.
The minister is going back to the interpretation clause. The word "package" covers pretty nearly everything, it means even an ordinary wrapper.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the package is sealed.
How could a basket, for instance, be sealed?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are sealed sometimes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the minister considered fixing a time from which this section shall begin to apply, or is there some general clause in the Act covering that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I intend moving a general clause afterwards.

Has the minister considered the desirability of making provision as to when these clauses shall come into effect? If not, I would suggest that after the word "package" on line 17 the following words be inserted "on and after July the first, 1921," or some similar provision. The object of my suggestion is to allow a reasonable time for the disposal of goods already manufactured and for using up the stock of printed labels in the hands of the manufacturers.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend evidently did not hear the answer I gave to the leader of the Opposition. I stated that I intended moving an amendment later on which would deal with that matter.
Would not ,the words I have suggested cover the point?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I can cover it in a better way.

Producers of maple
syrup very often seal their bottles simply with a cork, and the bottles bear the name and address of the producer. Would such a bottle be regarded as sealed? It would be very difficult for a farmer away back in the woods to state these particulars upon the outside of the bottle.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think- they seal the bottles.
They cork them.
I do not see any reason why they should not put the weight on. There is no reason why they should not be prevented from deceiving, any more than anybody else.
They do not deceive.
They very often do, I can tell my hon. friend.

It is highly desirable
from the standpoint of the lawyer that any Act should contain all its terms within itself, particularly an Act dealing with criminal offences. If a man should go to the minister's office-supposing the hon. gentleman ever should be obliged to go back to his practice and advise people on questions of law, and ask him a question about this Act,-the minister could not answer him simply by referring to the Act because he would find it mentions "regulations" which are not contained in the Act, and [DOT] which are not to be found in libraries. I submit that as much as possible should be put in the Act itself. It can be done, I think, particularly in a case where we describe what the punishment shall be. That would enable us to do away with regulations to a very great extent.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I quite agree that it is
desirable, so far as possible, that the Act should be complete in itself, but in an Act of this kind it is not possible as a practical proposition to put in all the details that may be required in regulating matters of this kind. The Orders in Council-and I think provision is made later on for this- should be published in The Gazette. They relate to regulations the violation of which constitute an offence, and they are always available on application to the department, I am only adopting the procedure which is universal in Acts of this kind. It is necessary to supplement the legislation by suitable regulations.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is one further
amendment necessary, in order to exempt from the operation of this clause packages of standard size as provided for in the Meat and Canned Foods Act. The Meat and Canned Foods Act provides for the sale of goods in packages of standard size. I therefore move to amend this clause by adding:
Provided also that nothing In this clause shall be taken to require the statement of weight, measure or number upon containers or packages of standard size as provided by Orders of the Governor in Council under the Meat and

Canned Foods Act, and provided further that the Governor in Council may make regulations deferring the operation of this subsection for such period as he may prescribe with regard to bottles containing mineral waters, ginger ale, ginger beer, or other common beverages ordinarily known as soft drinks.
" The latter part of this amendment appears to be necessary to meet a condition which the manufacturers of these forms of liquid refreshment find existing in Canada to-day. They say it is not possible to get the necessary supplies of bottles for ordinary bottling purposes, the glass being so scarce a commodity at the present time, and they have therefore been compelled to buy supplies of second-hand bottles in the* United States. The different states of the Union have different standards in the sizes of these bottles. Drinks are sold in pint bottles, so-called, but the bottles are not all of the same size, and the manufacturers state that at the present time they are not able to comply with the Act owing to their inability to procure bottles of a standard size. We are therefore deferring the operation of this clause for thre years to meet that situation that exists in Canada to-day.
Does this include milk bottles?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is no difficulty
about milk bottles.
Milk is a soft drink.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not in,lthe sense intended in the Bill.
I do not wish to be obnoxious, but I think you are killing your general section by this special legislation.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am simply deferring
the operation of this clause to make it possible for the industry to put itself in a position to comply with the law.
Will this provision apply to preserve bottles and bottles of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
Preserves are sold in sealed bottles.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The classes of bottles are -limited by the language of the amendment: "Bottles containing mineral waters, ginger ale, ginger beer, or other common beverages ordinarily known as soft drinks." It is in connection with these particular classes of bottles that the difficulty arises. There is a variation in sizes and it is found impossible at the present time to secure bottles of a standard size.
How does the minister propose to get over the fact that very small bottles are sold for the same price as the larger-sized bottles?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am free to say that the representations made to me in connection with this matter only strengthen my conviction of the importance of this section, because it is clear that bottles substantially differing in the amount of content are sold on the market as pint bottles.

Does the minister not think that if there are transgressors who sell'small bottles at the same price as large bottles he is giving them too long a tether in allowing them to continue in this state of illegality for three years?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They wanted seVen years, because they said that that was the ordinary life of bottles. I am not giving them the full period they request, however.

Is it the intention to
regulate the size of brandy bottles? I understand that brandy is sold in what are called "reputed quart bottles," as well as in imperial quart bottles. Is it the intention that henceforth it shall be sold only in the larger bottles, so that those who buy this drink may not be defrauded of the full quantity for which they pay?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am quite sure that all hon. members will sympathize with my hon. friend in the misfortunes he has suffered in the past in being taken in with regard to the brandy bottles he has been buying, but it is not my intention to make any special provision in that respect. My hon. friend will have to exercise his own ingenuity and skill, when he goes to buy a bottle of brandy, to determine whether it contains an imperial quart or the other measure.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The other evening some objection was taken to the use of the words, "exaggerated claims," in subsection (e) and I consented to have the word " exaggerated" struck out. If there is any objection to its restoration I shall not press the matter, but I find that the words " exaggerated claims " are in the American Act, and in other Acts of a similar character to this, with a view to meeting conditions such as will readily suggest themselves to hon. members. I think the Act would be better with the word in.
Who will decide whether a claim is "exaggerated" or not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The court before whom
the matter comes for decision. I move that subsection (e) be amended by replacing the words " or exaggerated " so that the clause may read as before.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 14-regulations by Governor in Council:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move to add to subsection (a) the following words, "or the Meat and Canned Foods Act " so that the clause as amended will empower the Governor in Council to make regulations:
Prescribing standards of quality for and fixing the limits of variabilities permissible in any articlf of food or drug the standard of which is not otherwise prescribed by this Act or the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
Was section 15 passed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

I was going to suggest to the minister that perhaps sections 14 and 15 might be consolidated, seeing that they both relate to regulations, one set of which are to be made by the Governor in Council and the other by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The only difference in
the two sections is that under section 14 the regulations must be published in the Canada Gazette. Those would be regulations the violation of which might result in conviction under the Act, and they must therefore be published in the Gazette. The other regulations are matters of internal arrangement, describing the duties of inspectors, the tariff of fees, etc. That was the reason why I left them separate the other evening.
Subsection (d) of section 15 is very broad.
We have not got through with section 14.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on section 14 now.

By section 14, subsection (b) the Governor in Council is given power to prescribe "what the colour, size and contents of such label shall be." I do not think the word "colour" should stand. It should be struck out. That is going a little too far.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Colour is a very important factor in the situation, although I intend to move a substitute for that clause. Let me give my hon. friend the illustrations

that have come to my own notice. Some use a yellow label and print the words they desire the public to read in black on yellow. They print the words that they do not desire the public to read and which are necessary to truthfully describe the article in golden letters on a yellow ground. The buyer does not read the words in gold because they are not conspicuous or noticeable and he is mislead by the discripfcion on the label. Another practice that has toome under observation is the use of a red coloured label on which the words that are intended to, be distinct are printed in black while the words that are not intended to be distinct are printed in brown, the brown on the red not being conspicuous while the black is. They have in the department scores of these labels all of which are clearly intended to deceive, and will deceive, unless1'a person is exceedingly careful in looking most minutely at the label. This matter was discussed with representatives of the manufacturers, and I move as a substitute for (b) the following:
Requiring a label to be attached to any article of food or drug designed to prevent the public, or the purchaser from being deceived or misled as to the character, strength, quality or quantity of the article.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Mr. iSEXiSMTTH: I suppose that under clause 14, paragraph (a) it would be possible for the Governor in Council to regulate the size and weight of eggs whether sold separately or by the dozen?
Mr. MIDDLETiRO: Would not that be covered by section 6, which says that the articles shall be "so packed, marked or labelled" as not to be likely to deceive any person with respect to their true nature?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is true. That section lays down the general principle and section 14 provides for making general regulations regarding all these matters. I also wish to amend section 14 by deleting subsection (c). I do it with some regret, but strong objection has been raised to the clause. On the other hand manufacturers have said to me that they consider it a valuable clause in the interest of honest business. But there is a strong objection to it, and so for this year I have decided to move to have it deleted.
From whom does the objection come?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Leading manufacturers all over the country have urged objection to

it on the ground that it is going too far in regulating the details of their business.
Agreed to.
'Mr. SEX SMITH: lit is under clause 14 that the Governor in 'Council regulates the weight of a dozen of eggs. There are regulations now prescribing what shall be the weight of a dozen of eggs, or of one egg and they were published in The Canada Gazette a year or two ago. Does it come under this section?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

I am very much interested in the decision of the minister in regard to this clause but I can really hear only a very little of the .conversation that goes on with regard to this Bill. I believe that other hon. members at this end of the Chamber will corroborate what I say in that regard. I would like to know what the decision is. Has the minister decided to eliminate subsection (c) of clause 14?
Mr. ROWiELL: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That amendment has been carried.
I cannot hear what is going on from where 1 sit.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should like, with the permission of the committee, to add a subsection to section 15, to be subsection (e). It is as follows:
The Governor in Council shall have power to make regulations:
(e) tor deferring the operation of any portion of this Act until July.l, 1921, when necessary or expedient to allow the disposal of stock on hand.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well it may be by them, but hon. members will realize that frequently it is very difficult to get the evidence upon which to determine that there has been adulteration of food. I am sure all the members of the committee will agree that every facility should be given to prevent fraud of this kind in order that the people should have good and wholesome foods, and to discourage food adulteration that may be prejudicial to the public health. The manner in which the department gets evidence is not infrequently in the form of information that it will be wise for them to inspect certain premises, or a certain, man's place or plant, because of what is reported to be going on there. The department gets the information, and upon investigation finds that adulteration is going on and a prosecution is instituted. Under those conditions the provision is made that half the fine shall go to the informer. Such a provision has proved of value in prosecuting people who are seeking to violate the law and to do things to the prejudice of the public interest, and I think it would be a mistake to. eliminate it because of the difficulties in getting evidence otherwise.

I would like to ask
what is to prevent any evil disposed person from treating sugar and water, or taking butter and mixing oleomargarine with it and putting it on the market. It seems to me that a crook who gets half the fine could get the best of any man in the country if he was afforded opportunities for doing so. There must be restrictions in some direction. In the district of Montreal the Inland Revenue officers have done their duty very well, but I .think under such a provision as this we shall have more 'trouble than we can deal with, if we allow this kind of information to be proffered by irresponsible people.

I suggest that this

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend raised the question whether some further procedure should not be provided under which a summons should be issued in the regular form for the calling of the third party before the court. I took the matter up with the Department of Justice, and they are of opinion that the clause as it stands is sufficient for the purpose. It is the same as the existing law and has been in force for some time. Prosecutions have been carried out under its provisions; the third party has been brought in, and I am informed that the procedure has never been questioned.

This clause provides that if a man charged with an offence proves his innocence and is acquitted, he shall be liable to pay the costs of the prosecution. That provision is unfair and un-British and should not be incorporated in the Bill.
Is that not qualified by the latter part of the subsection?

The accused has to pay the cost of the prosecutor if he is acquitted; then he has to take proceedings against the third party. He Should not be compelled to proceed against any one else in order to clear himself of the charge laid against him; that is unnecessary and unfair.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That matter was discussed at length when the Bill was previously in committee, and on that occasion two or three amendments were made which, while not having the effect suggested by my hon.
friend, to some extent met the point which he has raised. We cannot consent to strike out the whole provision, for the simple reason that the man i$ guilty of violating the law; he is selling something contrary to the law. We permit him to escape the consequences, and the costs too, if he does two things,-if he establishes to the satisfaction of the magistrate that he bought the goods as being of the same character, quality, etc., as that on which he sold them, and also brings before the court, in the manner provided in the clause, the man who is responsible for selling them to him. That has been the law, as I said before, for many years, it has been found to be a salntory provision and to facilitate the enforcement of the law and the work of the department in reaching the party who is really responsible for the fraud on the public.

I think the framer of this Bill has proceeded along entirely wrong lines. He has proceeded with the idea in mind that the entire commercial community of the country are immoral; that they are always looking for an opportunity to deceive and cheat the public, and that there is really no honesty among them. That is an entirely wrong position for the Department of Health to take, and they should adopt other lines. I do not know the tenor of the amendments that were made to this Bill when it was before the committee before, and it would, therefore, be impossible for me to discuss the subject intelligently at this moment; but I take issue with the Minister of Health (Mr. Rowell) when he says that it should be necessary to proceed in the first instance against the retailer who is handling this merchandise. If the goods in future are parcelled up, labelled and branded as the minister maintains in this Bill that they must be, then the merchandise itself will establish the source of their origin. It should, therefore, not be necessary for the department to proceed against the retailer who is entirely innocent, who has no knowledge of the exact condition under which the goods were manufactured; and if it is found by the department that the merchandise is defective in any respect, then it is the manufacturer who should be proceeded against and penalized, and the retailer should be only an incident in the prosecution as a witness against the manufacturer. This clause is a most pernicious one and should not be retained in the Bill. The fact that it has been in a former Act that is on the statute books, is no ground for its continuance. That the law has been wrong in the past is no reason why the law should be

continued in the present Bill. We are here to remedy any wrongs that exist at the present time, and I, therefore, move that this entire clause be struck out of the Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It would not be in

Then I move that subsection 1 of section 17 be amended by striking out all the (words after the word "prosecution" in the twenty-ninth line on page S of the Bill.

Mr. Chairman, I am
afraid I shall have for once to disagree with my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow) and to agree with the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell).
You are wrong.

I do not think I am, because I think the House will agree with me. The paragraph which the hon, member wishes to strike out is, as I understand it, not new law at all; it is law which is recognized in our Criminal Code in a large number of sections. The rule is that where a special defence is to be put in, the party who intends to avail himself of that special defence must give notice in writing to the prosecutor of his intention so to do. The prosecutor, in the absence of any such notice as that, will have his witnesses in court prepared to prove' the facts that he sets up, that is to say, that the goods have been misbranded and so on. This is a notice to the prosecutor that he must bring other testimony, testimony for which he would not be prepared unless he obtained this notice. I do not see that the defendant is going to suffer any hardship. The defendant, if he be a wise man, iwill naturally as soon as he is served with an information and a 'Complaint, consult his lawyer. His lawyer, who is supposed to know the law-that is a supposition, I will admit-will turn up section 17 of this measure, and on glancing at section 17 he will find that all that it is necessary to do is to notify the prosecutor that he intends to take advantage of that section and to prove that he obtained the goods in good faith. I do not think that works any hardship upon the defendant, and if the notice is not given, that works a hardship on the prosecutor. For that reason it seems to me that this clause of the Bill ought to go through as presented to the House by the minister.

I take exception to the position taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) in this respect. He claims that this provision is amongst the Acts of Parliament, and on the same ground as held by the minister, he claims that it should continue. My hon. friend is a lawyer and so is the Minister of Health, but there is *a difference betwen lawyers and men of common sense, sometimes. I quote no less an authority than the ex-leader of the Opposition for that statement. There is often a difference betwen lawyers and men of common sense. -
Does the hon. gentleman claim to have a monopoly of the latter?

I have it in common with a number of my friends who are not lawyers. The. Bill makes provision that all of this class of merchandise shall be branded in a certain way; that the goods shall be put up in certaimshaped packages. The style of package, the colour of the wrapping, even the colour of the printing and the size of the type to be used are prescribed, and the name of the producer must be on the package in no uncertain manner; even a fictitious name will not be tolerated. Therefore, there should be no hardship in compelling the prosecutor, the Government's agent, to investigate that feature of the matter himself, and to go direct to the person responsible for the adulterated foodstuffs and the material that is supposed to be covered by this clause. Why should the Government impose a hardship on an innocent party when they have within their own jurisdiction the means of going direct to the party responsible? That would be direct action that is so much desired by my hon. friends to my left. Direct action would deal most effectively with the situation; it would remove from the retailer the odium of defending a prosecution of this kind where he is innocent, because he is not the manufacturer, and consequently under the provisions of the Bill not liable for the penalty, if the section is properly worded. I think it is only fair and reasonable,- notwithstanding the fact that this provision is in the Statutes of Canada, that is should be .struck out of this Bill.
Amendment declared lost.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I might state that the rule concerning the vote of the chairman, in the case of a tie, is .that he should always volte in such a way as to leave the matter open for further consideration. Therefore, as the hon. member (Mr. Pedlow) will have the right to move his amendment on the third reading of the Bill, I vote against the amendment, and declare it loist.

The hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) says that it is no hardship for the accused under this section to be proceeded against as in the section provided, that he has always at his elbow a lawyer who will advise him what to do. Possibly that is true of a cilty like Montreal and other large cilties, and the section might not work very much hardship there. But in the county of Victoria, which is a very .material part of my riding, there is no. lawyer at all. There are very few .criminals, m the county from Which I come, but if charges of this kind are made ag.amslt the people of Victoria county they will have to travel beyond its bounds to get -a lawyer and the
result will .be that this very convenient practice which my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) suggests would not be .resorted to. the farmer or the man who is accused would know nothing about the law, and the result would be that in nine cases out of ten a fine would be imposed and he would have to pay the shot. I do not think that is a desirable condition of affairs at all. This is supposed to be a court without technicalities into which any man can come and tell his story, and in which the magistrate deals with "the question upon its merits without any red tape of any kind, but that is not the case. But the main point which I raised the other night was as to the calling in of the third party. The minister and the hon. member (M.r. Jacobs) say that it is a common practice in criminal law to bring in a third party, and that they have the opinion of the Department otf Justice, on that point. There are two people in. the Department of Justice whose opinion I would respect. I have a great deal of respect for the opinion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), himself, and the greatest possible regard for the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, .and if the Minister of Justice or this deputy minister says that this is good and proper criminal procedure, one that has run
the gauntlet and stood the test before the higher courts, I will at once accept that opinion; but if i't is merely the ipse dixit of some clerk in the Department of Justice who has never had anything to do with the higher remedies in connection with criminal law, who never had a habeas corpus case before the supreme court or never went through the courts with a certiorari case, I would not have much regard for his opinion.
Whalt about a summary conviction?

I would like my hon. friend to point to one case. There are cases of indictment where you could plead insanity. That would be open to my hon. friend if he were indicted. That is one defence that can be put up. Or he can raise the point that the case was tried before, that this was a second trial. There is a technical term for it which I shall not quote not being a good French or Latin scholar. Those are the only cases I am aware of. There may be other cases, but my hon. friend has noit quoted any. My point is this. Our criminal law demands that every man who is arrested, or summoned, or haled to a criminal court shall be given a clear and distinct opportunity of knowing iwhat is the charge. That charge is laid before the magistrate in distinct terms, and the terms of that offence are conveyed to the accused in a summons or warrant, as the .case may be, so that before 'he comes into the court he knows what he is charged with. But here we have simply the vague procedure that he shall be called into court. I think the minister and my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) will search in vain through all the criminal procedure in this country for a case where a man has been criminally charged and brought into court and fined simply under the procedure that he shall be called into court. It is provided here that he shall be called mlto court as hereinafter provided, but I find no procedure provided, in this Bill. If it is provided, I shall be glad to hear it. My conception of procedure under criminal law is that there shall be a regular information laid, and that the accused shall be fully acquainted with the charge so that he can come to court and have an opportunity of answering the charge. The procedure here would not (stand the test if it were challenged before the courts. Having put before the committee my views as to the proper procedure in connection with criminal charges I have nothing further to say.

speechtext:

It still follows that the innocent party, after he has been convicted by the court, is compelled to turn prosecutor and bring an action against the manufacturer.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not the effect of the section at all.

The section will be almost without effect in practice, because in line 23 it is provided that the person accused "must have a written warranty to that effect,-' and must produce it.
Iar clauses in the Inland Revenue Act and, I believe, the Customs Act. Mr. EDWARDiS': May I ask the minister for some information in regard to the caption of this section? speechtext: Apart from legal phraseology, and to use the language of the street or the shop, "certiorari" is a proceeding whereby the proceedings in an inferior court are removed to a higher court, where their legality may be passed upon. speechtext:

speechtext: I think the latest jurisprudence has established the fact that there is always a certiorari where there is an excess of jurisdiction.

speechtext: Yes.

I presume it is useless to try to convince the minister of the desirability of omitting this clause 18. The minister is-well aware that only ten days are allowed for appeal. Under our provincial law the applicant has six months within which to bring certiorari. Under this Act a man may be badly treated by the bungling conviction of a magistrate, but if he allows the ten days to go by he has no right to appeal. He takes advice and finds that he has a remedy by way of certiorari. His lawyer will state a case, bring it before the judge, and have it reviewed. Thus he will have his remedy in that way. Why should that very handy and serviceable common law remedy be taken away?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The whole object of the
Bill is to secure the expeditious and effective enforcement of the law, and the law is for the protection of the public. If a man convicted has any real defence on the merits, or a case which he considers good at law, he can appeal under the provisions of the Criminal Code. The facts can be gone into on the appeal and the merits of the case determined. If he is guilty the conviction will be affirmed and if he is not guilty the appeal will be allowed. Surely in enforcing a law of this character it is not in the public interest that- a man >vho is really guilty should be permitted to escape punishment by reason of some technical error in the proceedings which might be removed from the inferior court* by certiorari. If there is any merit in his case he can get it adjudicated upon by an appeal under the code. In view of the fact that that has been the law for so long a period not only with reference to this lAcit but with reference to the Customs and Inland Revenue Acts, in order that these laws designed in the public interest might be enforced as against parties violating them, it is not in the public interest to eliminate this provision from the Bill.
If the magistrate is proceeding without authority the man still has his right of certiorari.

In the Quebec district
the court of King's Bench generally sits twice a year. speechtext:

in that case, just as it does in every other case that comes under the code.

Sometimes it is enlightening to say that we are doing the same thing as we did last year. But some of us have no great knowledge of the principle upon which this bonus was paid last year. Will the minister explain in detail what that principle was?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At the request of the Minister of Finance I will explain the basis upon which the bonus was paid last year, as the matter came under my observation. All employees in the inside and the outside service who were heads of households and whose salaries did not exceed $3,000 a year received a bonus. The maximum bonus of $420 applied to- all employees who ;were heads of households and who received less than $1,200 a year. That $420 was scaled down by gradual steps until at $3,000 the amount of the bonus was $60. The bonus diminished as the amount of the salary increased. As applied to salaries from $1,200 to $1,320, the bonus to those who were heads of households was $396; from $1,320 to $1,440, $372; from $1,440 to $1,560, $348; from $1,560 to $1,680, $324. I need not read them all; the .scale downward proceeds in that way until you reach those receiving $3,000 a year.
What about the smaller salaries?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All who received less than $1,200 got $420 if they were heads of households. For those who were not heads of households the maximum bonus w.a.s $252, which was paid to all who received less than ' $960, subject to the exceptions I Shall mention. Then, from $960 the bonus to this class was scaled down until it reached $60 to the salary of $1,800; no bonus was paid to any employee in the inside or the outside service who was not head of a household and who received $1,800 or more. The scaling down was gradual, just as in the case of those who were heads of households. That was subject to these exceptions: Any person not the head of a household and who was over eighteen and under twenty-one years of age received a flat bonus of $150; those 
under eighteen received no bohus. Employees who were receiving current rates of pay, who were paid .by the day or week, received no bonus.
Was not the bonus granted to such employees later?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not if they were receiving current rates of pay.
I think that some of them were granted the bonus afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If they were, they did not get it according to the terms of the regulations. There is no justification for paying a bonus to an employee receiving current rate of wages. The bonus was intended to cover the increased cost of living and was based upon a sum which was assumed to represent, to some extent at least, the abnormal cost of living due to the war. Any one receiving the current rate of wages would be assumed to have received in that wage what would be equal to salary and bonus in the case of the other employees of the service.
What does the minister mean by "current rate of wages?"

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Take, for instance, men employed as workmen-carpenters, I would say; men employed in the construction of this building. If such men were paid by the Government and were receiving the current rate o.f wages, they would not be entitled to bonus; they would be getting the same rate of pay as people outside the public service. I think there was one further qualification-the bonus was not paid to part time employees, as I understand it. It was paid only to those giving continuous service.

You would think that if a man receiving $1,200 a year or more needed the bonus, a .man receiving only $300 or $400 would be even more in need of it. Unfortunately such a .man is met with the statement: Oh well, you are not supposed to give your whole time to the service; therefore you are not entitled to the bonus. As a .matter of fact, I am informed by the minister of the department concerned, to whom I made application in the matter and who was kind enough to give me the information, that that class of employees are not getting any bonus. I think there is something to be said in favour of that class of man getting a bonus. If he is not getting a larger salary, that is presumably because the quantity of work he has to do is not very great. On the other

hand, that man, getting a small salary, very often finds it rather inconvenient to take other employment. The nature of his duties may be such that although he may not be required to work hard, he may be obliged to be around all the time. Let me cite the case of a sub-collector of customs who has to be on hand at all times if he does his duty and who gets $300 or $400 a year It he applies for a bonus, he is told that he cannot get a bonus because he is receiving such a small salary, but the man thinks that is a good reason why he should get a-bonus. I invite the attention of the minister to that class of employee because I think he has a fair argument for getting a bonus. If his duties were such that he could go out and take other employment, there might be some ground for refusing to grant him a bonus; but such men, owing to the .nature of their duties are not at liberty to take up other occupations in the broadest sense of the word, and I think a very good case could be made out in favour of their receiving a bonus.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member will, I am sure, realize that the reason why a man does not get a bonus is not because he is paid a small sum, but because under his contract of hiring with the Government, he has not to give his whole time to the Government; he is free to take on other work. There is a distinction between a whole-time employee and one employed a few hours a day.

A collector of customs
must be on hand day by day to respond to any business that may arise, and it is absurd to tell him that he can take other employment. Theoretically, he can, but practically he cannot. In many other classes of the service, a man might be able to take other employment. In this instance, the volume of work to be done is not sufficient to induce the Government to pay a large salary, but the conditions of the work are such that the employee is not as free as other men to take other employment. He could not go away from his community; he could not undertake to drive a coach; he could not do anything that would take him away from home. He has to hang around, even if there is nothing doing, in the expectation that something might arise. Where a man's duty is of that character, the fact that he gets a small salary is not a reason for penalizing him; it is a reason for giving him a helping hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I remember, when I
was Minister of Customs, the different cases
the hon. gentleman mentioned. 'Customs officers sometimes get as little as $50 and up to $300, but in every case some one is appointed who lives in the district, who has other business, or who really has this as a side issue. An office of that kind is open for the convenience of the public, and in every case the officer has something else to do. An officer of that kind is not appointed for the purpose of giving his whole time, and if I remember aright, the Customs Act mentions the fact-a man getting under $1,000 may be employed in other work. If you were to start giving this bonus of $420 to these men who are employed in doing other work outside, I do not know where the matter would end. Hon. members can see how much this bonus amounts to in regard to the permanent employees, and I do not see how we could be justified in considering these cases because these men are really not giving their whole time like regular employees of departments.

A man getting only $50 a year would be manifestly engaged in such a side business that the argument of my hon. friend would perhaps apply, but I do not think it is a fair answer to the sub-collectors of customs who are getting three or four hundred dollars. I do not think they are as free to go away and take other employment as the man who has a fifty dollar job.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There might be some exception to the rule, and I shall be very happy to consider the details of any cases the hon. member is kind enough to bring up. The matter is one of regulation.

In all these cases, I much prefer to go to the minister privately to bringing the matter up in Parliament. I spoke to the Minister of Customs about the matter, and he said that the general rule was that the men undertook that work as a part service and that he was very sorry he could not give them the bonus. I am, however, content to accept the assurance of the minister that the matter will be looked into.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
' My hon. friend is in error in one respect. It is true that reclassification is to come into effect as of the 1st April, 1919, under the Bill now before the House, the Civil 'Service Amendment Act; but the scale of salaries fixed in that reclassification was fixed, not on the present high cost of living, but based on the former schedule in the old Act, the former classification, plus the probable normal increase in the cost of living. In fixing the salaries in this classification, the Civil Service Commission intimated that in order to pay the 'Civil Servants what they would consider fair remuneration, it would be necessary to supplement them by a bonus, having regard to the present very high cost of living. Either that must be done, or the Civil Service Commission, in recommending a schedule of salaries to the Government and to the House, would have recommended a higher schedule than that included in the classification, and it was deemed wiser not

to fix salaries on the Ibasis of the present exceedingly high cost of living, because we hoped a year ago and two years ago, and still hope, although our hopes apparently are not likely to be realized immediately, that there would be a decided lowering in the cost of living. It was thought easier to deal with the matter by way of bonus pending a lowering in the exceedingly high cost of, living. I quite agree with my hon. friend that the time must come, and very soon, when the bonus should be dispensed with and the permanent salary fixed, but I think on the whole it is probably economy and in the public interest not to fix salaries at the present time, but rather to deal with the question in this abnormal period by a bonus.
Are we to take it for granted that reclassification has not yet come into effect?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I did not say that.
I am just asking the minister.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The reclassification is being put into effect day by day. The law is in force now as from the first of April 1920, and there is a Bill before the House to make it retroactive so that it shall be deemed as having been in force as from the first of April, 1919. That will be of real benefit to the service, because in many classes there is quite a mateiial increase in salary as compared with the old classification. This bonus is based on the reclassification, and is recommended to the Government as being necessary to reasonably supplement the salaries fixed in the reclassification.

What does the minister understand by "the head of a family" in connection with the distribution of the bonus? Bonuses are paid in some eases to some who are really not the heads of families, .while others who are practically the chief support of a family do not get the same amount of bonus. There has been considerable confusion in the past.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I regret that I have not here the definition of the head of a household, but I can tell my hon. friend in a general way what it includes. Every married man, every man who has a family to support is the head of a household, but it is broader than that. If a daughter working in the public service ii supporting invalid parents who have not other means of support she is deemed the head of the household for the purpose of the bonus,

and instead of getting the bonus which a single person would receive, she would receive the same bonus as a married person because in that family she is the supporting head of the household. I think it is true that in the administration of the bonus under the regulations which were worked ,out possibly theTe have been some cases where bonuses have been paid as to the head of a household where they should not have been paid. That is one of the regulations that is now under consideration with a view to modification, in order to guard against the payment of bonuses under conditions where it should not be paid.

Following that up-and
it was the point I had in my mind when I rose first-if the expenses of the household are evenly divided between two young girls, both working in the public service, would they both be classed for the purposes of the bonus as the head of a family, or only one of them?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

Did the Governor in Council modify the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission last year?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot recall in detail further than this: As a matter of fact, the recommendations or suggestions of the Civil Service Commission were discussed with the minister responsible for administering this branch of the service, last year the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and when a conclusion was reached as to what would be the most equitable system for distribution, the recommendation was made and the Order in Council based on that was put through. I do not recall that any recommendation made by the commission was formally changed. I think the matter was discussed and an agreement arrived at, which was then embodied in an Order in Council, that is as near as I can recall.
Are the recommendations made by the commission general in their application, or does the commission make particular repommendations with respect to certain individuals in the service.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are no recommendations relating to particular individuals in the Civil Service. The regulations are general in terms, and apply to all who come within the different classes provided. All that the regulations do is to define the classes, and the amount of bonus paid depends upon the class in which the individual falls.

I would point out that in the distribution last year there was a certain injustice because the bonus gradually decreased up to $3,000, and those receiving ' above $3,000 received no bonus at all. The civil servants whose salaries range between $3,000 and $6,000 deserve particular consideration. Last year Parliament was asked to vote an increase of $1,000 in the salary of the deputy ministers of the various departments. Formerly the deputy ministers had received $5,000 per annum, but with this increase last year they now receive $6,000. We did not find fault with the Government in taking that action, I think the increase was unanimously voted. But surely if the deputy ministers could not live on $5,000 a year, but required an additional $1,000 salary, the civil servants who receive anything between $3,000 and $6,000 should

also be considered. Generally speaking they aie men of great experience and of great value to the service, many of them having professional and. technical qualifications which would command a higher salary in the outside world than they are receiving with the Government. The evidence of this is that the Government has lost this year, as it lost last year, a number of civil servants possessing technical or professional qualifications. I would call the minister's attention to that point and would asik that those civil servants whose salaries range between three thousand and six thousand dollars be given some consideration in the distribution of the bonus.

Regulations for a cost of living bonus for employees in the Civil Service of Canada prepared by the Civil Service Commission.
Cost of Living Bonus.
Section 1. In addition to all salaries now, received by the employees in the Civil Service, a special cost of living bonus for the fiscal year commencing April 1. 1919, shall he paid to all persons employed in the Civil Service in Canada, in the groups named below, subject to the provisions and exceptions enumerated. Provided, that no section of these regulations shall be construed to mean that an employee qualified hereunder to participate in the bonus, shall receive a continued salary and bonus for the present fiscal year less than the combined salary bonus, and living allowance entitled to be received by the employee for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1919.
Bonus groups.	'

Group 1 (a) Any person the supporting head of a household, receiving less than $1,20>0 per year for full time service and not otherwise excluded by the provisions of these regulations, shall receive a bonus for the fiscal year of $420 payable in monthly instalments of $35 each. For the purposes of these regulations a married man supporting a family shall be considered the head of a household. The Civil Service Commission shall have power to make regulations to be approved by the Governor in Council, classifying as heads of households other persons, the sole support of dependents, who, in the opinion of the commission, are subject to responsibilities equivalent to those of the head of a family, and on the basis of such regulations shall have power to make rulings as to fhe receipt of bonus by persons coming under such regulations.
(b) Any person the supporting head of a household, receiving $1,200 or over and less than $3,'000 per year for full-time service, and not otherwise excluded by the provisions of these regulations, shall receive for the fiscal year, the bonus indicated or such person's salary group.

Section 5. In determining the income received by an employee all salary, wages, piecework earnings, and special allowance for all purposes except payment for overtime, received by the employee from the Dominion Government shall be included.
