(Section 6.-In the case of a person receiving living allowances, such as quarters, food, and so forth, in kind or in money, the value of such allowances as computed by .the head of the department and approved by the Civil Service Commission, shall be considered as constituting part of the total income received by the employee, but there shall be deducted from the bonus of the employee such proportion of the total bonus as the value of such living allowance may bear to the total income so computed.
Absences.
.Section 7.-Absences on leave with pay of the type customarily allowed by the department to salaried employees, but not to exceed one month in a six month period, shall not be considered as affecting the status of the employee as a full time employee.
Salaries in Excess of the Classification.
iSection 8.-Subject to the provisions of section I, an employee receiving, a salary in excess of the amount provided by the pending Civil Service Classification for the class in which he is employed, when this classification becomes effective, shall receive only so much salary and bonus total as would be provided by the maximum salary for the class plus such bonus as the bonus group of the employee would then entitle him to.
Time of Payment.
(Section 9.-Bonus shall be paid on the fifteenth day of each calendar month (or other regular pay-day of the department) for the calendar month preceding such pay-day. For new employees entering the service, current bonus shall be computed from the date of entering the service, provided that no payments shall be made until the employee has been in service a full month, and that employees remaining in the service for less than a month shall not be entitled to receive bonus.
Method of Payment.
Section 1-0.-Payments of bonus made under these regulations shall in each case be made by separate cheque or pay enevelope, specifically designated by the title '*Cost of Living Bonus."



Misrepresentation of Bonus Group.
Section 111.-Proof of wilful falsification or mis-statement of facts, of a nature intended to enable a Civil Service employee to obtain a bonus in excess of that to which he is entitled, shall constitute grounds for dismissal from the service.
Extinguishment of Bonus by Salary Increases.
Section 1,2.-In the case of any general increases in the class salary rates of an occupational group, the amounts of such increases shall be deducted from the bonuses paid to the members of the group receiving the increase. These regulations shall automatically cease to operate for any occupational group, or for all groups, when the amount of increases so given shall be sufficient to extinguish the bonuses for the group or groups.
Persons Receiving "Prevailing Rates."
Section 13.-Persons whose rates of pay is determined as the prevailing rate paid for similar work in the region in which they work, shall not be entitled to participation in the bonus.
.	Part Time.
Section 14.-Persons whose duties do not require their full time, or whose public functions are incidental to their occupation, or who are permitted while in the service to accept employment or engage in commerce or industry, shall not be entitled to participation in the bonus. Provided, that persons giving their full time to the service for periods of a month or more, shall receive bonus pro rata for the period worked, in accordance with the provisions of these regulations.
Revision and Interpretation.
Section 15.-The provisions of these regulations shall be subject to such revision and compensatory adjustment as may be equitable and necessary when the pending classification becomes effective for any portions of the service. For the purposes of departmental uniformity in administration, the Civil Service Commission shall make such application or interpretation of these regulations as may be necessary, subject to such rulings as may be made by the Governor in Council.

Prior to the reclassification the maximum salary of letter carriers was $960. What increase do they receive under the new classification? Are they still in receipt of $960, the wage paid "them when fifty cents purchased as much as a dollar does at the present time? It would seem to me that $420 would not be sufficient to make up the difference between the cost of living now and what it was iwhen $960 was regarded as an adequate salary for these men. It strikes me that i$420 is not nearly enough to make up the difference in the cost of living, particularly for a man with a family, and it is only the heads of families who are eligible for this allocation.

Under the old classification the salaries of letter carriers ran from $600 odd to $939, as I recall the figures. iThe maximum under the new classification

is $1,260, over $300 more than the old maximum. iSo that a letter carrier who was receiving the maximum say for five years prior to this classification will start in at $1,160 as at the 1st of April, 1919. If he had been receiving the maximum for five years he would be eligible for another $120 on the 1st of April, 1920, making $1,280; and then he would be entitled to this bonus. ,He would not get quite $420, because he would be receiving more than $1,200; but his salary plus bonus would give him $1,656, I think. The House will agree that no just ground of objection can be taken to that amount as the salary of letter carriers in Canada at the present time. I make this statement because there has been a good deal of criticism in the press in various sections of the country with reference to the salaries paid by the Government to letter carriers. I think that, under the reclassification, and with the bonus, the letter carriers come out about as well as any other class in the service, if not better.
Are they furnished ,with uniforms?
Yes.
Two uniforms?

I do not know. Hon.
members must bear in mind that in the *case which I have mentioned I have given the maximum. Those who have not been ;so long in the service will draw something less than the figures I have given, as also those who are not heads of households.

I must call the attention of the minister to the information .which is furnished the committee in the Estimates before the Chair. I think it is an objectionable way of legislating to put a few lines like these in 'an Estimate and give them the same force as an Act of Parliament; because it must be regarded as an ..Act of Parliament, otherwise the Order in (Council could not be based upon it. This :is a large amount of money, and all the information which is given us is the statement that it is for a provisional bonus .allowance for the Inside and Outside Services of the Civil Service to be paid to such persons and classes of persons and in such amounts and at such times as the Governor in Council may determine. I submit that this is a very objectionable way of making large expenditures of this kind.
We usually have Orders in Council based upon the statute and when we put that statute through the House giving the council power to make regulations the

substance of those regulations is largely set forth in the statute itself and we have a fairly good idea of the kind of regulations that will be made because they must be in compliance with the statutes. This is a very meagre basis indeed and affords very little information to the House as to what these regulations will be. After getting all the information I could for the minister I must say that I feel that I am very much in the dark as to how this money will be expended. We have a classification which nobody on earth seems to be able to comprehend, and with that incomprehensible system of salaries this is put into the hands of some poor man [DOT] and he is told to go to it and divide this money amongst hundreds and thousands of men and women employed in the Government. For a long time we have been trying to reach a proper basis for the Civil Service and after the very large amount of money that was spent on commissions,. and after engaging the very best talent we could get not only in our own country but in other countries, it is rather disappointing that we should be just as badly off as ever we were and that we must adopt these Orders in Council and [DOT] proceed by the old rule of thumb by which we granted this bonus last year. , Perhaps the minister will tell the committee how much more than the $12,500,000 we pay to the class of civil servants who are to get this bonus. We may at some time get that information. Possibly it is not available to the minister now. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) told us this afternoon that he est evidence of economy should show itself est evidence of economy should show itsell in the ranks of the Government we should try to encourage it. I would like to see if any economies can be effected in regard to the Civil Service as well as in other lines by reason of the new blood that has been introduced into the Finance Department. Men at the first blush are more shocked with enormities than they will be after they become familiar with them, and therefore let us hope before the new minister gets crusted,, hardened and accustomed to these enormities we may have some slight improvement and that he may inquire how much money we are paying out to the civil servants. We have been for years talk-11 p.m. ing about reform in the Civil Service.
This classification was to do a lot of weeding out, and to do away with the supernumeraries and a great many people who were drawing money and whose services we could dispense with in order that they 821
might employ themselves in some other way. The other day we had this subject up irf the House and I think we had some promise from the Government that the matter was to be taken up and that some results were to follow. But, we are going on as if this promise had never been made. This is an opportunity for the Minister of Finance to tell us if any such results are going to be brought about. Is there any cutting down in the pay sheet? Are there less employees in these different departments now than there were a year ago, or is there any hope that the promise that was made to Parliament will be implemented by a cutting down of the numbers? I should not be asking the new minister all these things but I have no mercy at all on the President of the Privy Council because he knows everything and he can tell us all these things.

In reference to the remarks (made by the present leader of the Opposition-
Mr. MeKENZIE: No.

The acting leader of the Opposition?
Mr. MeKENZIE: Not even that.

I would say that I do not think he has assisted the Minister of Finance very much in cutting down the expenses of the Civil Service. It may be possible to cut down the pay-lists but it seems to me that a lot of those in the Civil Service remember quite distinctly that when this bonus was first adopted it was called a "war bonus:" Since the war is ended it is called a "bonus." I think we have a pretty fair intimation that it is the intention, with the classification, to make it a permanent part of the salaries of those in the Civil Service. I have a pretty fair idea as to what the members of the Government are up against living here in Ottawa and surrounded as they are with those who are in the Civil Service. I believe it is the duty of the members of this House to speak out frankly what they have in their minds. When we treat the civil servants as martyrs and declare that they are not receiving as much for their services as they should and that we should adopt an old age pension and a superannuation allowance for them, we do not set a very good example to the rest, of the country, especially at the present time. We know the hours of labour that we have fixed for those in the service and it has proven to be an example for every one

not in the service but engaged in other occupations to strive to reach. About a six and a half hour day is the maximum for the civil servants of this country. Reference has been made to the salaries that have been paid to the postmen and letter carriers of the cities and it is said that it is not sufficient to enable them to live as they should. That is one of the peculiarities of the Civil Service. People will almost break their necks to get in, and once they get in they seem to have a great deal of time at their disposal to agitate for an increase in their salaries. There should be no re-ason why those in the service who feel that they should do better elsewhere, or that they are not receiving, what they think they are worth should stay there. Why can they not get out of the service and take up some other occupation as other people do if they do not feel satisfied with the position which they have?
I fail to see why once persons are taken into the Civil Service of the country they should remain there continuously for the rest of their lives and should receive consideration that no other class in the community receives. That is certainly the case in regard to the hours of labour. It is a downright shame that members of this House who are here so late cannot go to a department until an hour in the morning when some people have nearly half a day's work completed. It is only then that you will find the civil servants filing into their offices.
I believe that if any other business in Canada, or any other country for that matter, were conducted as the public service of this country is conducted it would go, bankrupt within a year. ;I believe there should be a thorough re-organization of the whole public service of this country; that businesslike methods should be applied in connection with it; that a great deal of the overlapping which we find in the various public departments should be done away with; and that there should not be so much rivalry and jealousy between ministers as to whether some other department is encroaching on theirs or not.
Start with the ministers.

A new department of the Government has been organized very recently and T notice that the sum of nearly $1,000,000 is provided in the Estimates for it. We have now a condition of affairs in Canada that demands the close attention of

the people's representatives in Parliament. It may not be popular to say what I am now saying, but I am only expressing what I feel as to things that I have seen and noticed for many, many years, and T must say that I believe there is too much humbug in connection with this advocacy of the increasing of the salaries of these people who are in the service and are being kept there for the rest of their lives. If these people are not satisfied let them get out.
Reference has been made ' to the letter carriers. It does not require a tremendous lot of physical energy or brains to be a letter carrier. And yet what do you find? In similar occupations that require a very great deal more physical energy, and where there is competition for instance on an undertaking that is let by contract, you can secure more work for less than half the money that these people are receiving. That is quite apparent to all and to every1 one. Yet we are advocating passing of an item of over $12,500,000, without very much consideration and with more empty benches in this Chamber, possibly, than we usualy see. We have become so familiar with talking in millions, that we think these things ought to slip through without very much consideration. Now I have some .sympathy with the Minister of Finance who has recently taken over the work of that department. He has a heavy task on his hands and we ought to lend him all the assistance in our power to help cut down expenses and to put the finances of this country on a sound and stable basis. I do not believe that we are fair to the minister, or fair to the Government, in continually leading up to and harping on the idea that there should be increases all along the line. I believe that there should be dismissals, and dismissals by the thousands from the Civil Service, and that efficiency should he the tests and my opinion is that under the plan we have adopted in connection with the Civil Service Commission we are going to have a much more rotten system in the future than we have at the present time. I have no sympathy with this commission Dusmess as I have seen and as I judge it from the short experience I have had as a member of this House. 1 believe that the Government must be held responsible for the administration of the affairs of the country and that they cannot delegate that responsibility to any commission. Now, Sir, we purpose under this re-classification to enable the Civil Service Commis-

sion-acting on the advice of some people who have been hired at a very heavy expense to the country for a long time-to deal with the public service. We are kept in the dark as to what really should be done, and we are now continuing to the civil servants what we were told was merely a temporary war bonus. The war is ended but the bonus is not. We are now calling it a bonus and talking about making it a part of the permanent salaries of those in the Civil Service. People who enter the Civil Service of Canada do not need to think that they are occupying a superior position to those who are carrying on in other walks of life. Yet you would almost imagine they do think so from the attitude which the/ have adopted and the tactics which they are pursuing. I have a distinct recollection that about a year ago when Parliament met we had a strike in a certain branch of the Civil Service. The members of that branch thought they had the Government right by the throat and that it was impossible for the Government to do anything or to carry on. We found the Government endeavouring to get the printing in connection with the business of the House done outside of the Civil Service. But could that be managed? No, Sir. We have an organized body in the Civil Service to-day that are carrying on and are dictating to the Government and are getting away with it every day in the week. Have we arrived at a time when it is only organized bodies that are going to be considered, and that the great mass of the people of the country, who are unorganized, are not to receive any consideration? I do not like to speak in this way, it is not a pleasant task to me, but 'I am merely expressing my views as I feel them. I believe it is in the public interest, and it should >be of some value to the Government, for us to render them some assistance in withstanding these onslaughts that are being continually made upon them by organized bodies who are threatening to do this and to do that and to put the Government in a position practically of being at their mercy. And the Government are very much at their mercy unless the members of this House stand by and support them when they endeavour to do such things, instead of trying to make a little political capital out of these matters.
I wish to ask the minister in charge of the Bill whether slide masters in the Outside Service will be given this bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would depend entirely, I should think, on a man's position and the amount of his regular pay. If he was in the regular employment of the Government, in the Outside Service, and was paid less than $1,200 he would get a bonus of $420. If he was the head of a househcild and unmarried he would get a bonus of $252.

I wish to draw the attention of the Finance Minister, in connection with this bonus question, to the case of Mr. John Mullen who has been slidemaster, under the Department of Public Works, at High Falls, on the Coulonge river. This man has been in the employ of the Government for twenty-one years, but has now been dismissed, with only one month's salary, after that long period of service. Will Mr. Mullen be entitled to any part of the bonus being paid under this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The bonus is
payable monthly in addition to the regular salary. If a man was being paid a .salary he would get it; if he was paid by day's wage he would not get it. If the wages of the man to whom the hon. gentleman alludes as slidemaster were the ordinary rate of wages paid to the district he would get no bonus at all.

This man has been in the employ of the. Public Works Department for twenty-one years. He started at something like $400 a year, and I understand the wages he has lately been drawing on a yearly basis amounted to $900. He was dismissed because the works he was employed on were taken over and given to the lumbermen. He did not receive any notice what-ever, but was merely notified that he was to be paid one month's wages. I want to know, when a vote such as this is being obtained for the Inside and Outside Service, if the case of a man in such a position is . being taken into consideration. He has served the Government for twenty-one years and is now sixty-eight years of age. I therefore ask why he should be dismissed without any further notice than he received, and without any bonus or superannuation, or any consideration whatever, when we are voting the .sum of $12,500,000 to supplement the salaries of employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is not a pension plan; it is merely the appropriation of an amount to supplement monthly pay cheques. The slidemaster referred to, if employed on regular salary, should have got his bonus for last year. But this item has

nothing whatever to do with the question . of retiring officials or anything of that kind.

There is a great deal
of force in the observations of the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), who points out that in view of the number of empty benches this evening we should not pass an item of $12,500,000; that opportunity should at least be given to every member of the House to express his opinion with regard to it. I am sorry that the minister does not appreciate the willingness of the experienced member for (South Oxford to give him some assistance in cutting down the heavy expenditure in connection with the Civil Service. Hon. members on this side learned long ago that it was like pouring water on the proverbial duck's back to make any such suggestions or present any such philosophy to the present aggregation composing the Government, and we have to some extent given it up. I am glad that the member for South Oxford, who4 has a right to expect that his representations will receive more consideration at the hands of the Government than ours do, has taken this role; and few members in the House can present their views more logically than he can present his. I hope, therefore, that the Government, while they may be disposed to ignore the suggestions made by hon. members on this side, will not take the responsibility of refusing to pay attention to the observations of such an important supporter as the member for South Oxford.
I suggest that the Minister of Finance [DOT](Sir Henry Drayton) become serious for a moment. The amount involved in this item is quite a substantial one. It was not brought up until after ten o'clock this evening, when many members, particularly on his own side of the House, had left the Chamber, possibly having no idea that a money vote was to be placed before the committee for consideration. The leader of the Opposition is not here. We have acting as leader the exMinister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), a very capable gentleman, but the leader himself is not here, and the general attendance in the House is not large. I think, therefore, that it would be a prudent and gracious act on the part of the minister to let this item stand until hon. members shall have had more opportunity of giving it consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am very grateful to hon. members for their assistance and support;.we need a lot of it, too. I welcome it whether it comes from South Oxford or

from the Atlantic coast. There is no doubt that we ought to economize; that we have to economize wherever we can. But there are some places where you cannot economize-except, perhaps, on matters of time. The hon. member has referred to the leader of the Opposition. I understand that this matter was taken up with the leader of the Opposition and that he did not think there was any . reason why it should not be taken up and disposed of this evening. After all, there is nothing that we do not know in connection with this matter. We all know that the cost of living in going up instead of going down. We all know that we are not enlarging the bonus which was given last year. We all know what the basis of that bonus ^as. We all know that this is nothing but the payment of a bonus having regard to salaries of employees fixed by statute. We know also that these salaries, whether fixed by the reclassification or previously, were fixed when the cost of living'was very different from what it now is and when payment for services in outside employments was on a very different basis from what it now is. This is not a permanent matter, as some hon. members seem to think. The payment of the amount made up by the salary as fixed plus the bonus would be permanent if the classification were based upon the total of the two. It is thought to be cheaper to keep the salaries down as much as possible and to continue this bonus until the cost of living drops, as we all hope it will. It is much easier to stop the payment of a bonus than to reduce salaries which have once been increased. Personally, I should be only too delighted to accede to the request of the hon. member that the consideration of this question be postponed. But a lot of cheques are due to be sent out to-morrow, and if no real object is to be served by delay it would be a great pity for hon. gentlemen to hold them up.
Mr. tOQPP: I do not think the minister will suggest that hon. gentlemen on this side are holding up this item.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all.

But he must realize that the item is one of considerable importance and involves a large sum of money. My hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland), in a careful and well-reasoned address has suggested many things to the Government that they might well take into consideration. He suggested that a new department had been established by the Government which he characterized as being unnecessary, if not useless. He

did not tell us what department that was; it might be well for the minister to give us some information with regard to it and to say whether he feels that, as the member for iSouth Oxford has suggested, that department is unnecessary and useless. I do not quite agree with all that the member for South Oxford said; nevertheless he furnished a good deal of food for thought. Of course, we now talk in millions where a few years ago we talked in thousands, and possibly on that account the amount of this item does not seem so large. But $12,500,000 is a very large sum of money, and I feel that the committee should have some further information with regard to the matters put before the Government and the Finance Minister by the member for South Oxford.

I should like to take
issue with the hon. member for Oxford [South (Mr. Sutherland) who seems to be pf opinion that because the war is over, the war bonus should cease. The hon. member should understand that in spite of the fact that the war is over, fhe cost of living is still going up. How in the name of common sense should the war bonus cease while the cost of living is going up? The war .bonus was, as I understand it, introduced so as not to disturb the scale of wages. This is the principle that is adopted by all large commercial companies. As regards wages paid to civil servants, I am of opinion, from the few inquires that I have made, that civil servants do not receive the same standard of wages which commercial companies pay, and if we wish to get efficiency coupled with economy in our civil service, we must pay more wages in qrder to get the best employees. If any commercial company were to adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) and discharge their employees and continue to pay wages below the ordinary scale of wages being paid by other companies, that commercial company would soon be obliged to go out of business; they would have no employees. Economy then must be accompanied by efficiency. I hope our new Minister of Finance will introduce into his department, at least, some reforms along the lines that have been suggested. There is only one way to get economy coupled with efficiency, and that is to get the very best employees possible to do the necessary [work and to pay them a scale of wages equal to that paid by commercial companies.

Will keepers of lights on
the sea shore be entitled to this bonus?
[They are employees who receive smaller pay for their services than any other employees in the Civil Service. Are they going to be considered, or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry to say I cannot mention the names of the different classes of employees that will get the bonus. The general rule, as the hon. gentleman will remember, is this, that if an employee is a salaried employee, that is, he is somebody that is working for the Government and giving his whole time to the Government "and is not engaged upon other work, he gets the bonus, whether he works Inside or Outside, so that if the lightkeeper to whom the hon. gentleman refers falls within that class, he will get a bonus.

Many of these men spend about eight or nine months of their time in the service, and they receive from $160 to about $300. They received this when the cost of living was very low, and they are still receiving the same salary without any increase. Some of them are far from their homes on islands or beaches or places like that, and I think they should receive either an increase in salary or a bonus.

There is another class of civil servants that has not received any bonus so far and these men are in about the same class as the lightkeepers. There are on some islands, in particular the quarantine stations, telegraph offices that are open about nine months during the year, and telegraph officers are on those islands during that period. In the winter they live in their homes on the islands where there is practically nothing for them to do in the winter time, so that they are really devoting all their time to the service. I do not understand why last year they did not receive any bonus at all. I suppose this year, when reclassification is reconsidered, such an officer, who gives nine months of his time to the 'service and who is let out in the winter when there is nothing for him to do, will receive a bonus to keep him going.

I should like tcf call the
attention of the minister to a class of public servants who have been sadly neglected in the past, a hard-working class, a class which works more hours a day than any other public servant and which I think ought to be recognized either by way of bonus or by an increased indemnity. I refer to the members of this House.
Oh, oh.

I am quite serious. This may not be the right time to bring the

matter up; but on another occasion I may be out of order, and now that we have such a large number of members present, it might be well to bring the question up. I think members of this House are entitled to an increased indemnity, and above all they are entitled to exemption from income tax if nothing else can be done for us. If that cannot be done, we are entitled to deduct from our income tax returns the amount of our actual expenses incurred in Ottawa. As regards that, I think I will have the general support of the committee. With regard to the question of increased indemnity I shall have pretty general support of the members, not in this House-in the lobbies, at home, and possibly amongst their friends, but hardly in public. I wish, however, to bring this matter to the attention of the minister, and 1 should like him to inform the members of the committee if, in arranging their budget for the coming year, members may count on a substantial increase in their indemnity, as a bonus.

I wish to join with the hon. /member (Mr. Leger) who spoke a little while ago in favour of the lighthouse keepers. I have several of these public servants in my constituency, and I understand from the minister that in order to receive a share of the proposed bonus, they must come within certain regulations. I understand that one of those regulations is that they must devote all their time to the public service.
I know for a fact that before the war, and before the cost of living had reached its present level, those men at least in that portion of the St. Lawrence opposite my county had to report for duty in the spring on the first of April, and they closed their lighthouses on the first of December. They are now bound to open their lighthouses on the first of April instead of the 12th, and have to' remain at work as late as the 23rd of December, and I understand that they are liable to be called1 up for service' at any time during the year. I do not know if* they would be eligible to share in the bonus, but at all events I would suggest that as they are so poorly paid they should be allowed to participate in it.

I notice by the
Public Accounts, which I have in my hand, that for the year ending March 31, 1919, at the little farm the Government are running on the outskirts of this city the amount paid for farm labour was $120,525.44. Can the minister give me any idea as to what portion of that is made up of the war bonus?

I refer to the Experimental Farm. I also notice that on the farms in the province of Quebec some $71,000 odd was spent for farm labour. That does not include foremen or any of the men drawing the high salaries, but is for the actual farm labour. I am not surprised at the hon. member (Mr. Reid) taking exception to reducing salaries when the cost of living is going up, bu? in view of the fact that the farm labour on the land being farmed by the Government costs about five times as much as thfe proceeds from that land. I am inclined to think that if that system is going to be applied throughout the whole country the cost of living will go a great deal higher than it is at present.

Will the rural
mail carriers share in this bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rural mail carriers are paid under contract. This bonus merely applies to those drawing salaries which we ourselves fix. What is being done in connection with the rural mail carriers is this: In cases where they think 'they have tendered too low and are' not being sufficiently paid the Post Office, on request of the mail carrier, cancels the contract and gives him a chance to tender again along with any other tenderers there *may be.

I do not think there is a class of public servant who are more deserving that the rural mail carriers. My hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) has said that they take these contracts at competitive prices. More than that, if their tender is considered too high by the department the contract is not given. The department sets a limit of so much per mile, I think it is now $30 per mile, and they will not give a contract at a higher price. The mail carriers have to provide their own horse and rig, and it must be remembered that the price of feed has almost doubled in the last few years. These men certainly deserve an increase, and if they are not to participate in the bonus, they should be given a percentage increase on their contracts of at least 33J per cent.

I should like to point out the great discrepancy that exists between the remuneration given to the rural mail carriers and to the letter carriers. It has been stated on the floor of this House that the letter carriers may receive a maximum of $1,260, and on top of that a bonus approximating $400, which would bring their total remuneration up to about $1,600. The rural mail carriers, on the other hand, are doing their work for anything between $500 and $900, and in many cases they have to supply two horses and a rig. They receive no bonus whatever. I notice that the minister takes refuge behind the statement that bonuses are only granted to those who are receiving fixed salaries, and that the mail carriers work under contract. That is perhaps true, but the Post Office Department are practically setting the salaries received by the rural mail carriers, Although they advertise for tenders in almost all cases, any post office inspector who feels that a tender is to high so informs the tenderer, offering him a smaller amount. In most cases this is the way the agreement is made. The work is not actually done by tender. I wish to point out the great difference there is between the salaries received by the letter carriers and by these men who are doing much more arduous work.

I wish to say a word or two in support of remarks made by several members in connection with rural mail carriers. In my county contracts were given a few years ago at low prices, and mail carriers discovered afterwards that they could not fulfil such contracts with profit and they could not afford to lose money with the Government. The minister told us a moment ago that in cases of that kind new tenders weTe called for and contracts were given at higher prices. My experience in my own constituency is that whenever a price was asked which showed a reasonable profit for the mail carrier the inspector would generally interfere and see to it that the contract was not given to that tenderer. In this way we generally had poor service. I think that if these bonuses are to be given to the civil servants on the principle that the cost of living is much higher now than before the war they should apply to every one including those in the rural constituencies. The rural mail carriers should also share in the grant, and if they did I think there would be ft great improvement in the service.

What portion of
the $400,000 paid for farm labour on the experimental farms is war bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think any of that would be war bonus. Farm labourers should be employed at the current rate of wages. If they are taken on

at the current rate of wages there should be no bonus at all but, of course, if they are not taken on at the current rate they get a bonus.

To continue my remarks in regard to the rural mail carriers, I would point out to the Minister of Finance the fact that very generous subsidies have been given to steamship lines to carry mails. Now, if the Government have the means to give as high subsidies as we are giving to the steamship lines, I think they can afford to 'be generous to our rural constituencies and accord them somewhat better treatment than they now receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will observe that those subsidies have been considerably reduced.
Very good news,

Something has been
said
Carried.

Hon. members had
better be patient; this is an important item, and if any hon. member thinks that twelve and a half million dollars is not worth talking about he can retire. We on this side regard this item as one of great importance, and as we are here to represent the people we are prepared to put our views before the minister. Hon. members may regard these things as being too trivial to engage their consideration, but I am not one of that class and I am willing to stay here and talk to the minister about the business of the country. I was about to say, in connection with the system of lighthouses in this country, that there is in my riding a very important island called St. Paul's, on which there is a little colony of lighthouse keepers with their families. These people cannot by any possibility engage in any other kind of work, being fourteen or fifteen miles from the shore, and the island being very small there is no kind of industry. I should like to know if the men who are so occupied on St. Paul's island will come within the operation of the bonus, I do not know what their salaries are. Can the minister inform the committee what is the minimum salary that entitles one to the bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The smaller the salary the bigger the bonus, so long as the man is an employee of the Government.
I understood the President of the Privy Council to say that there was a place where it stopped.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Upwards, not
downwards.

I think downwards,
too.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; the smaller the salary the bigger the bonus.

Then I must have misunderstood the President of the Council, because the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) raised the point that a customs officer getting only $250 would not participate in the bonus because his salary was too small.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because his was only part employment.

The minister told us that a matter of great importance was economy of time, and I think he referred indirectly to the delay that might be experienced in passing this item. I do not wish to obstruct the minister in this legislation, but I wish to inform him that this Supplementary Estimate was brought down only to-day, and I got it in my mail only to-night just before coming to the House. We discussed several Bills in the evening, and this matter was brought up at half past ten. It is now five minutes to twelve and we have discussed dor less than an hour and a half an item involving twelve millions and a half. So that I do not think we have wasted any time as the Minister of Finance seemed to imply a short while ago.

With reference to the Experimental Farm employees, I notice . that a bonus of $200 has been paid in almost every instance in connection with the amounts paid to these men ranging from $800 to $1,200, but the bonus does not vary with the salary. While I am on my feet I may say, with reference to the rural mail carriers, that in passing this item, which provides for a bonus to all others in the Civil Service, we ought to have some assurance that something will be done for these men. Their condition is certainly deplorable, and they have been fully expecting the Government to show them the same consideration as is given those in other branches of the public service. There is no gainsaying the fact that these men do their work for less than one half what is received by others who do easier work; and the fact that there is competition in this branch of the service and none in the other is no justification for keeping these men down. It is true that in many instances they are men who do not attach any great value to their orwn service. Frequently

they are crippled in some way and are anxious to earn a few dollars in order to keep themselves. I think we should really have some assurance from the minister, before putting this vote through, that the Government will endeavour to make some provision for these people under the conditions that exist to-day.
Does the Order in Council that the minister has read providing for the distribution of this bonus apply to the distribution this yean or is it the one that applied to the distribution last year?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is the Order in
Council on -which the distribution was made last year. The Minister of Finance has stated that the same general principles would govern the distribution this year except that there were certain modifications under consideration, one of which my hon. friend himself brought to the attention of the committee.
Does the hon. gentleman refer to the Order in Council that applies to this item or to the bonus of last year?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Order in Council providing for the distribution of last year.
Of the year 1919?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of the fiscal year 1919-20. The same general principle will apply to this distribution, although it will be subject to modification.
But this vote is for the year which has passed, 1919-20?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Np, it is for 1920-21. .
I understand that the regulations for the distribution of the bonus for this year are not finally drafted.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
I would like to know undeT what regulations this distribution is going to be made before we are called upon to vote that amount en bloc.
The Minister of Finance declared that the cheques were practically ready.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What I said, or at least what I intended to say, was that we were proceeding on the old basis but that the old basis might be changed in a few details. We have prepared our cheques under last year's Order in Council and on the old basis.	.

,

*
But they are the cheques for this year's bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, it would be for this year, but the cheques cannot go out unless this is authorized.

That is a practice that should not be tolerated. The practice of distributing money that has not been voted should not be tolerated by the new minister. The item says that the money shall be distributed under regulations yet to be framed. Up to this date the Governor in Council [DOT]could not make any regulations in regard to these particular items. They might draft them, but they would have no effect. We have been told that regulations are to be made for the distribution of this item which the House has not yet passed. Why does the minister say that before this item has been passed regulations have been made providing for the distribution of this large amount of money and that the cheques are ready to go out? That is riding roughshod over the principles and privileges of Parliament. What is the use of going through the farce of asking us to pass this vote if the cheques are made out, the distribution is made and we are not consulted about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cheques will only go out and the distribution will only be made when the House gives its assent. We are simply ready to do it.

It should not be done in advance. The regulations should be here as well as the item so that we will know on what principle this distribution is to be made. There are two sets of wage rates with which we could deal. There was the rate of wages that the civil servants received before the Civil Service Act came into force. There is a new scale of wages which has come into force since the first of April, 1919. The old regulations were made under the old rate of pay, but now we do not know whether this distribution is to be made under the new system or the old. Will the minister tell us? The distribution of last year took the present Civil Act rate of wages. Do they now take that same 12 p.m. rate of wages as a basis for the distribution of the rate of wages as provided by the new Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand it-I- may be entirely wrong-the bonus is paid on the ordinary salary cheque. These cheques have to be prepared. If the bonus was not written into them it would mean that separate cheques would have to be

provided. It saves a lot of work to put both the bonus and the salary upon the same cheque. It is much better to write out one cheque.

Which scale of wages has been taken as a basis of distribution, the old salaries or the new salaries under the Civil Service Act? The different classes of salaries would provide a different basis for the distribution of this vote. I am asking the minister which of these two classes is taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I understand it the recommendation of the Commission is based upon the new classification. It would have to be based upon the new classification, according to the judgment of the Commission or the amount to be provided this year would require to have been greater.
Why was this item not in the Main Estimates? It was evidently well understood that there was going to be a bonus when the general Estimates were prepared?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The whole question has been a matter of very anxious debate. If I could have got rid of the bonus altogether the bonus would have been got rid of. If I had been able to see any fair way of dropping it, it would have been dropped. It has been a matter of very anxious debate. It was considered only two days ago by Council.

History is repeating itself. We were told in this House last year by the hon. member for Regina (Mr Cowan) that he and a few of his colleagues forced the Minister of Finance to do certain things; for instance, to drive the axe into the tariff as effectively as possible. I see that the forcing business is going on with the new minister just as well. He wanted to do certain things when he brought down his main Estimates, but since then he has been forced to do something else that he had no intention .of doing. In view of the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland) that we ought to help the minister, I think we should help him to some stilts for his backbone.
Would the minister say if the amount of the bonus granted this year is the same as that granted last yegr?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the same as last year.

If the House is asked to vote the same amount as last year how

does the minister reconcile this with the declaration of his desire to economize?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Replying first to the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) I do not know that the ktilts which he is thinking of would help very much. I am learning about matters all the time, and I have learned one thing, that in connection with salaries and the cost of living it would be an injustice to civil servants to withhold the bonus. It was because of finding out the fact that an injustice would have been worked had the bonus been withheld that I am taking the position that I do to-night.
With respect to the question of my hon. friend (Mr. Cannon) as to the matter of economy, I think the hon. gentleman will agree that the cost of living this year is higher than it was last year. If he does not agree, I am sorry to say I am afraid the facts all show that the cost of living this year is higher than last, and that there has been an appreciation of some ten per cent. Now the re-classification of salaries is not on to-day's values; it is based on a lower standard of living than we have today, thus requiring the addition of this bonus to bring it up to a proper proportion.

I want to be well understood by the minister; I would not like the impression to be left in his mind that I am opposed to giving a bonus to the civil servants. For some reason or other-it may be the fault of the Government or the fault of somebody else-living is much more expensive in Canada now than it used to be, there is no douibt about that. Should salaries be increased, dr bonuses given and salaries remain at the same position as they were a few years ago? That is a question for the Government to settle and not for me to decide. However, I put the question to the minister as to whether the bonus given this year was the same as that given last year. His answer in the affirmative proves that his claim to economy has not been carried out, because if the total bonus is the same as last year how can the Government have economized? I know personally that some employees have been dismissed from the service-lots of them; for instance in the Printing Bureau, in the Militia Department, and in the Naval Service. The number of employees in these departments has decreased. Some of them have been dismissed, and others have resigned. How does the minister explain to the committee that notwithstanding these resignations and these das-

missals, the country to-day will pay the same amount as it paid last year, and *despite the fact that each individual is not getting any more, because the basis for the bonus will be the same this yearbarring a few details of no importance-as it was last year? I would like the minister to give that explanation before this vote is passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer is very simple. The hon. member for Lotbin-iere (Mr. Vien) raised a point which I thought some hon. gentlemen, at least, agreed with. His point was that during the whole course of the war nothing had been done for the man in the technical service, the engineer. There is the man who is getting between $3,000 and $5,000. It is because the question of looking after that very class is under consideration that the amount was put at the figure that it now is, but there is no intention-I would like to quiet the hon. gentleman's mind upon that score-oif increasing the individual bonus.

Will the minister tell the committee what amount has been laid aside to be distributed as a bonus to those people who have not received a bonus in former years, and what amount has been laid aside to distribute as a bonus to the employees who enjoyed a bonus last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand the amount that is under consideration in connection with the extra class is $240.
How much will that amount to in round figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have only a rough estimate.

Hofw can the minister make a rough estimate when he does not know how many there will be to benefit?
'Sir HENRY DRAYTON: This is not a rough estimate by the Government; it is-based on a report from the Civil Service Commission. The Commission have gone over the matter and discussed it. It is their figures that we have. I could not, I am sorry to say, tell exactly how many there are in the class mentioned by the hon. member for Lotbiniere as against the number in the other class.

Where is the report to
which the minister refers? could it be laid before the committee? It is a very important question and I think the committee should be enlightened on that point.

The cheques must have been made out from some list. I think it would be valuable to have that list on Hansard. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) told us that the maximum salary for which a bonus was given was $3,000. I think he told us that the men getting $3,000 received no bonus but that the bonus was applicable in an increasing degree as the salaries fell below that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the matter now stands all bonuses cease at $3,000. At its maximum the bonus applies to low salaries below $1,200 and then scales off. The proposition still under consideration is as to whether or not the bonus should be continued from a $3,000 to a $5,000 salary.

The cheques are not
yet made out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I have been so accustomed to talking in terms of fifty cents and a dollar, and receiving such scathing denunciation from members on the Government side, that this question of a vote of $12,500,000 is almost beyond my comprehension It seems to me that I have a grand opportunity to give a lesson in economics to hon. gentlemen opposite, and I would ask the minister how he reconciles the bonus system for the mail carrier in the urban sections with the treatment meted out to the mail carrier in the rural district?
If I understood him correctly, the minister said that the cost of living had not materially increased. I wish to point out that the cost of material has very much increased during the last year, particularly to the rural mail carrier. Feed for the animals that have been driving on the trails this winter has cost much more than it formerly cost. They are paying more for their oats; they are paying $60 to $70 per ton for hay which last year they bought for $20 and $21-in no case more than $26. These rural mail carriers on our western plains have had two months more travelling than usual this winter in heavy snow, heavier than usual in the West- and they have asked me if they could not under some arrangement receive extra pay. They did not suggest the manner in which they should receive it; I am satisfied that they are prepared to accept it whether it is given to them in the form of increased salary or in the form of bonus. In any case, they are justly entitled to some consideration. I have also received communications from persons in that country complaining about

the rentals paid by the Dominion Government for the buildings in which the business of the Post Office Department is carried on. When we are voting this sum of $12,500,000, we should provide that each employee should get his or her equitable share of the bonus. I wish to put myself on record as being in favour of giving to these rural mail carriers their just share of this appropriation, because to my positive knowledge they have, through no fault of their own but through act of Providence, had more difficult conditions to work under than lias ever before been their experience.

The minister has told us that the reason why this item is not in the ordinary Estimates is that it had given rise to anxious debate. Where? It could not have given rise to anxious debate on this side of the House; the anxious debate must have been in Council. Judging from the , attendance of -Government members, they do not seem to show much interest in the matter. I gather from the remarks of the minister that the debate in council was an anxious one. Why so? Judging by the warmth of the minister's remarks I assume that he as Minister of Finance was opposed to this bonus; that he as the man who is best posted on the subject of our financial condition was not in favour of it. But other views prevailed, and the minister comes down before the committee to-night and asks us to vote $12,500,000. I feel tonight as the minster felt up to this afternoon; I am not in favour of voting $12,500,000 unless I am convinced that we can afford to do so. I certainly shall not vote for the adoption of this item unless I am shown conclusively how the money will be spent. I do not want that money to be squandered. I do not want that money to be , wasted. Enough millions have been wasted by the present Government. During the war it was easy for gentlemen on the other side to say that they wanted to spend so many millions of dollars for the welfare of the country and the defence of the Empire. That argument is worn out. The war is over, we are back to times of peace; we have come back to -constitutional practice. Gentlemen on the other side will be called to account for every penny that they spend in Canada. This item provides that $12,500,000 shall be spend in accordance with regulations passed by the Governor in Council. That may be sufficient for the committee as a whole but it is not sufficient information for me. I want more than that. I want the Government to do as regards this item what they have to do [Mr. Gould.1
when the bring down the ordinary Estimates. When an item for $1,000 is asked by the President of the Council (Mr. Kow: ell) or by the Minister of Immigration and -Colonization (Mr. Calder) we have a right to ask them to tell us exactly how every dollar will be spent. I shall vote for this item only when I know how the appropriation will be distributed. The minister says that a certain amount has been laid aside to be distributed among the employees who receive more than $3,000 in case the Cabinet should decide to give them a bonus. I want to know whether or not the Cabinet have decided to give them a bonus. If they have, what will be the amount? How many dollars of this $12,500,000 will be given to these employees? We are not children in this House. We represent the people. This country is overburdened with debts- The Minister of Finance -does not know where to find the money to meet the needs of the public service. Every week he is expected to make his Budget speech and explain how we are going to meet necessary expenses and conduct the ordinary affairs of the country, but the Budget is delayed. The minister is pondering that matter; he has been doing it for months. The committee should not vote an item of this importance until the Government gives us the necessary information. What will be the amount given to those who receive salaries exceeding $3,000. What will be the amount given to the Outside Service? What will be the amount given to the Inside Service? Will employees outside of those receiving $3,000 a year receive bonuses who did not receive them last year? It is only fair to ask that that information should be given to the committee. I do not know how the other members of the committee feel about it, but I am sick and tired of voting items without having any information,-of signing blank cheques for the Government. These officials who sign cheques without knowing whether or not the money would be voted insult Parliament and show gross negligence of constitutional practice. It is about time that these employees should know that the masters of the public exchequer of Canada are the members of the House of Commons; not officials of the Government. So far as I am concerned, unless I have the necessary information, I will oppose this item.

I thought the minister
was hunting a few minutes ago for information as to what amount of this appropriation is to be applied on bonuses to the people mentioned iby my hon. friend (Mr. APRIL 15, 1920
Cannon). Surely, the Government are not serious in asking Parliament to pass in a lump sum this item of $12,500,000 which they placed on the Table to-day, without stating what proportion of it is to be applied as mentioned by my hon. <friend or what policy the Government have decided upon, or without any further information as to what the Government are prepared to give at the present time. That is most unreasonable; it is certainly unfair to members of this committee; it is unfair to the Opposition, and it is unfair to the Minister of Finance for him to come down to this House and show that he does not know any more about his Estimates than to say that he does not know what this amount is to be expended for. The minister should surely be in a position to furnish us with the information before he asks that this item be passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like
very much to meet the wishes of the hon. gentleman. Perhaps the best thing to do would be to treat this vote just like the ordinary Estimates and simply vote one- sixth in the same way as is done with the ordinary Estimates in order to carry oh. That leaves the whole thing open for any information hon. members desire to give or any further remarks they desire to make.
Will a loan be necessary to cover the payment of this bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that
question has already been ruled out of order, firmly, definitely and finally.

The Chairman has not
done so to-night.	[DOT]

While in the other
Estimates we were asked to pass only one-sixth, I understand that in this case the minister has asked for the whole amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For one-sixth.
The suggestion he makes to conform with the rule and ask for one-sixth and thus leave the matter open, might be a fair solution of the matter.

In case the one-sixth is
passed to-night, is it possible that we shall have further discussion at some other time on the remaining five-sixths?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
When this item comes up again, I suppose the minister will have that list and general information as to the balance of the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move that this item be amended by inserting the words "one-sixth of the" . at the beginning and by substituting for the amount $12,500,000," the amount "$2,083,333.33."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.	.
Item as amended agreed to. ,
Resolution reported, read the first and *second times and concurred in.

stagedirection

speechtext:
